subtopic_detail: rapidly enlarging vascular birthmark over the upper eyelid obscuring part of the visual axis at ten weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10-week-old girl whose parents point out a red raised lesion on her left upper eyelid. It was a faint pink patch at two weeks and has grown noticeably each week since.

The lesion is now 15 mm across, bright red, raised and compressible, and it partly covers the upper half of the pupil when she is upright and relaxed. It is not ulcerated and not bleeding. She was born at term, is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile. There is no other lesion on the skin, no bruit over the liver, no stridor and no other abnormality on examination, and the rest of the eye looks normal with a symmetrical red reflex. Her parents say a relative was told to leave a similar mark alone because it would disappear on its own.

data_table.Examination: 15 mm raised compressible bright red lesion of the left upper eyelid partly covering the upper pupil, no ulceration, symmetrical red reflex
data_table.Growth: Weight tracking the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Other findings: No additional cutaneous lesions, no hepatic bruit, no stridor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her at the 12 month immunisation visit for regression
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for most of these lesions because the great majority involute without treatment, but one that obscures the visual axis can cause deprivation amblyopia within weeks at this age. Waiting until 12 months risks permanent visual loss on that side. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma

options.text: Apply topical timolol gel twice daily and photograph the lesion weekly at home
options.rationale: Topical beta blockade is useful for small superficial lesions in non-critical sites, but penetration is insufficient for a deep or bulky lesion and absorption near the eye is a further concern. It will not shrink a periocular lesion quickly enough to protect vision. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma

options.text: Refer urgently for oral propranolol with cardiovascular screening and ophthalmology review
options.rationale: Periocular location with interference in the visual axis is one of the standard indications for systemic treatment, and oral propranolol produces visible shrinkage within days to weeks during the proliferative phase that continues to around five months. Referral includes pre-treatment cardiovascular assessment and ophthalmology involvement for amblyopia management. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and neck before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for large segmental facial lesions, where associated structural anomalies of the posterior fossa, arteries, eye and sternum must be sought, or for lesions with functional airway concern. A solitary localised eyelid lesion with no other findings does not require it before treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment as the definitive management of the lesion
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser has a role for ulcerated lesions and for residual telangiectasia after involution, but it treats only the superficial component and does not debulk a proliferating lesion. It cannot clear the visual axis within the window that matters. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks of life, proliferate until around five months and then involute slowly over years, so most need nothing beyond explanation and review. Treatment is indicated when the lesion threatens function or life, when it ulcerates, or when it will leave significant disfigurement, and a periocular lesion obscuring the visual axis is among the clearest functional indications because deprivation amblyopia develops quickly at this age. Oral propranolol is the first line systemic therapy and produces rapid shrinkage during the proliferative phase, given after cardiovascular assessment and with feeding and hypoglycaemia advice for parents. Imaging is reserved for large segmental facial lesions or airway concern, and topical timolol is limited to small superficial lesions in non-critical sites.
key_points: Proliferation continues until about five months, which is the window where treatment works fastest
Functional threat, ulceration and disfigurement are the indications for treatment
A periocular lesion touching the visual axis risks deprivation amblyopia within weeks
Oral propranolol is first line; topical timolol suits only small superficial lesions
explanation.pearls: Ask where the haemangioma is before deciding whether it can be left alone: eyelid, nasal tip, lip, airway and perineal lesions all need same-week referral, and for one touching the visual axis oral propranolol plus ophthalmology review is urgent rather than something to revisit at the next immunisation.

subtopic_detail: loss of consciousness after a sudden fright with pallor preceding the event and a brief stiffening
stem:
You are the doctor in an emergency department. A 16-month-old boy is brought in after an episode at home. He bumped his head lightly on a table, looked startled, went pale and limp within seconds without crying out, and lost consciousness for about 20 seconds with some stiffening of his arms.

He came round on his own and was back to normal within a few minutes, with no drowsiness and no confusion afterwards. His mother says this is the fourth similar episode in three months, always triggered by a sudden fright or minor knock, and always with pallor first. He is thriving and has normal development. His diet is mainly cow milk, about a litre a day, with limited meat. He is afebrile and examination is normal with a soft abdomen, no murmur, no organomegaly and a normal neurological examination.

data_table.Episode description: Sudden fright or minor knock, pallor within seconds, limpness, 20 seconds of unconsciousness with brief stiffening, rapid full recovery
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 68 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (15-150), electrocardiogram with normal intervals
data_table.Development: Normal milestones, thriving, diet mainly cow milk with limited meat

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the mechanism, treat the iron deficiency, and give first aid advice for episodes
options.rationale: Reflex anoxic episodes triggered by fright or minor pain, with pallor preceding collapse and rapid recovery, are benign vagally mediated events and iron deficiency is a recognised precipitant whose correction reduces their frequency. Parents need an explanation of the mechanism plus practical advice to lie the child flat and not to shake or resuscitate, since the child recovers spontaneously. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.text: Start sodium valproate and arrange an outpatient electroencephalogram within four weeks
options.rationale: An antiseizure medicine is indicated for epileptic seizures, which are not preceded by pallor triggered by a fright and are usually followed by a postictal period rather than immediate normal behaviour. Treating these episodes as epilepsy exposes him to a hepatotoxic and teratogenic drug for a benign condition. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.text: Refer for cardiac electrophysiology study to exclude an inherited arrhythmia syndrome
options.rationale: An inherited arrhythmia would be suggested by episodes during exertion or swimming, a family history of sudden death, or an abnormal electrocardiogram, none of which are present with normal intervals on his tracing. Invasive electrophysiology is far beyond what a classical trigger-and-pallor history requires. (Source: RCH CPG: Syncope)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Syncope

options.text: Admit for continuous video electroencephalographic monitoring to capture a typical event
options.rationale: Prolonged monitoring is useful when episodes are frequent and the diagnosis genuinely remains uncertain after a careful history. Here the trigger, the pallor before collapse and the immediate recovery make the diagnosis clinically, and events triggered by fright are unlikely to occur on demand in hospital. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.text: Advise the parents to prevent all episodes by avoiding any situation that startles him
options.rationale: Avoidance is impossible to sustain and drives restrictive parenting that harms the child's development more than the episodes themselves. Explanation with first aid advice achieves far more than attempts to eliminate every trigger. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

explanation.summary: Reflex anoxic episodes are vagally mediated asystolic events in young children, triggered by a sudden fright, minor injury or unexpected pain, in which the child goes pale before losing consciousness. Brief stiffening or a few jerks from cerebral hypoxia are common and often lead to a mistaken diagnosis of epilepsy, but the sequence of trigger, then pallor, then collapse, with rapid full recovery and no postictal phase, distinguishes them. Iron deficiency is a recognised and correctable precipitant, so a full blood count and ferritin are worth checking, and an electrocardiogram is reasonable to exclude a long QT interval. Management is explanation, iron repletion when deficient, and first aid advice to lay the child flat and let the episode terminate on its own.
key_points: Pallor before the collapse, with an identifiable trigger, separates this from an epileptic seizure
Brief stiffening or jerks are hypoxic and do not indicate epilepsy
Iron deficiency is a correctable precipitant and repletion reduces episode frequency
An electrocardiogram excludes a long QT interval; further cardiac testing is rarely needed
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent what colour the child went and in what order things happened: pallor that precedes the collapse after a bump or a fright is a reflex anoxic episode, and the treatment is explanation plus iron repletion if the ferritin is low, not an antiseizure medicine.

subtopic_detail: thin midline membrane joining the labia minora in an asymptomatic preschool girl with a normal urinary stream
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother noticed that her vulva looks different while helping her in the bath. The mother is worried that something is missing or has been damaged.

The girl is toilet trained, passes urine in a single forward stream without spraying, and has never had dysuria, discharge or a urinary tract infection. On examination, with the mother present and after explaining what you are doing, the labia minora are joined in the midline by a thin translucent membrane, with a small opening anteriorly through which urine passes. The vulval skin elsewhere is normal in colour and texture, with no thickened white plaques, no fissures, no bruising and no bleeding. Growth and development are normal.

data_table.Examination: Thin translucent midline membrane between the labia minora with a patent anterior opening, surrounding vulval skin normal
data_table.History: Continent, single forward urinary stream, no dysuria, discharge or previous urinary tract infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric gynaecologist for separation under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Surgical separation is reserved for adhesions causing urinary obstruction, recurrent infection or symptoms that persist after topical treatment, and it carries a high recurrence rate until oestrogen levels rise at puberty. Operating on an asymptomatic girl with a patent anterior opening exposes her to anaesthesia with nothing to gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions

options.text: Prescribe topical clobetasol ointment once daily to the vulva for four weeks
options.rationale: A potent topical corticosteroid is the treatment for vulval lichen sclerosus, which presents with thickened white plaques, fissuring, itch and bruise-like haemorrhage, none of which are described here. Applying it to normal vulval skin risks atrophy without addressing the fused membrane. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis

options.text: Apply topical oestrogen cream twice daily for six weeks and review the response
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen does separate adhesions, but it is used for girls with obstructive symptoms, recurrent urinary infection or persistent local discomfort, and it commonly causes local pigmentation and occasionally breast budding. Starting it in an asymptomatic girl treats the parents' anxiety rather than the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions

options.text: Report the finding to child protection services as a possible sign of sexual abuse
options.rationale: Labial adhesions are an ordinary consequence of the low oestrogen state of childhood combined with local irritation, and they are not a marker of abuse; bruising, tears, bleeding or an abnormal disclosure would be. A notification made on this finding alone would be both distressing and unfounded. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Child abuse

options.text: Explain the finding, advise simple vulval care, and review only if symptoms develop
options.rationale: Adhesions that do not obstruct urine flow need no active treatment because almost all separate spontaneously as oestrogen rises around puberty, and many resolve earlier. Explaining the mechanism, advising against soap and bubble bath, and naming the symptoms that would warrant review is complete management. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions

explanation.summary: Midline fusion of the labia minora is common in the low oestrogen years between infancy and puberty and is usually discovered incidentally by a parent. The decision point is whether the adhesion is obstructing: a single forward stream, continence and no history of urinary infection all indicate that it is not. Asymptomatic adhesions are managed with explanation and vulval care alone, since the great majority separate spontaneously and any treatment carries a high recurrence rate before puberty. Topical oestrogen, and rarely surgical separation, are reserved for obstruction, recurrent urinary infection or persistent symptoms.
key_points: Asymptomatic labial adhesions need explanation and vulval care, not treatment
Urinary stream, continence and infection history determine whether the adhesion is obstructive
Topical oestrogen is reserved for symptomatic or obstructive adhesions and recurs commonly before puberty
White thickened plaques with fissuring and bruising point to lichen sclerosus rather than simple adhesions
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to describe the urinary stream before deciding anything about labial adhesions: a single forward stream with no post-void dribbling and no previous urinary tract infection means the adhesion is non-obstructive, and the correct plan is explanation plus soap-free vulval care with review only if symptoms appear, not a six week course of oestrogen cream.

subtopic_detail: repetitive vomiting and pallor two hours after a first feed of rice cereal with no urticaria or wheeze
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 6-month-old boy is brought in pale and floppy. He has vomited more than ten times over the past hour. His mother says he was completely well this morning and had his first ever bowl of rice cereal two hours before the vomiting started, mixed with his usual formula which he has taken since birth.

He has no rash, no lip or tongue swelling, and his breathing is quiet with no noisy breathing or cough. He is lethargic but rousable and his hands feel cool. There was a similar but milder episode three weeks ago, two hours after his only previous taste of rice cereal, which settled at home over an afternoon and was attributed to a stomach bug. He is afebrile, and there is no diarrhoea, and no one else at home is unwell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176 beats per minute, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and lethargic, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, chest clear with no wheeze or stridor, skin free of urticaria or angioedema
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 15 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glucose 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms intramuscularly into the lateral thigh, repeated if needed
options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is the treatment for immunoglobulin E mediated anaphylaxis, which is defined by acute skin or mucosal change with respiratory or cardiovascular compromise, typically within minutes of exposure. The two hour delay, quiet chest and entirely normal skin place this outside that pathway even though the child is shocked. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Normal saline 20 mL/kg as a rapid bolus with intravenous ondansetron, then reassess
options.rationale: This presentation is cell mediated rather than antibody mediated, and the shock comes from massive fluid shift into the gut, so the treatment is aggressive volume replacement with an antiemetic to break the vomiting cycle. Boluses are repeated until perfusion is restored, and most infants improve within hours without any adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone after blood cultures, with a fluid bolus for suspected sepsis
options.rationale: Sepsis is the reasonable default for a shocked lethargic infant, but the child is afebrile, the illness began abruptly two hours after a specific food, and an identical milder episode followed the only previous exposure to that food. Antibiotics can be added if the course deviates, but they do not explain a twice-repeated food-locked pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Oral rehydration solution given in small frequent volumes with review in four hours
options.rationale: Oral rehydration is first line for mild to moderate dehydration in gastroenteritis, but this infant is shocked with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and is vomiting repeatedly, so the oral route will fail. Shock requires intravenous or intraosseous volume regardless of the underlying trigger. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone with a non-sedating oral antihistamine and observation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and antihistamines treat neither the volume depletion nor the underlying mechanism, and antihistamines are ineffective because histamine release is not the driver of this reaction. Relying on them would leave a shocked infant without the fluid that actually reverses the process. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

explanation.summary: Profuse repetitive vomiting one to four hours after a food, with pallor, lethargy and hypotension but no urticaria, angioedema or respiratory signs, is the signature of food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome. Rice, oats, cow milk and egg are the usual triggers in Australian infants, and the reaction is cell mediated, so skin prick testing and specific immunoglobulin E are typically negative and adrenaline has little role. The shock is hypovolaemic from fluid sequestration in the gut, and treatment is rapid isotonic fluid replacement with ondansetron. A previous milder episode after the same food is the historical clue that converts a presumed gastroenteritis into a recognised syndrome.
key_points: Delayed onset of one to four hours with no skin or respiratory features separates this from anaphylaxis
Treatment is 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid boluses plus ondansetron, repeated to restore perfusion
Skin prick testing and specific immunoglobulin E are usually negative because the mechanism is cell mediated
A repeat episode after the same food is the clue that the first was not gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: Ask what the infant ate two to four hours before the vomiting started, and whether the same food preceded a previous episode. Repetitive vomiting with pallor and shock but a normal skin and chest, twice after the same grain, is food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome: give 20 mL/kg saline boluses and ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg, not intramuscular adrenaline, and refer to a paediatric allergy service for a supervised food challenge rather than an adrenaline autoinjector.

subtopic_detail: developmental regression with microcytic anaemia and abdominal pain in a child living beside a smelter
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a regional hospital. A 2-year-old girl is referred with four months of intermittent abdominal pain, constipation and irritability. Her parents say she has stopped using the ten words she had at 18 months and now mostly points. The family moved 18 months ago to a house built in the 1920s, three streets from a lead and zinc smelter, and renovations stripping old paint were done while they lived there.

She eats little meat and drinks about a litre of cow milk each day. There has been no vomiting, no fever, no diarrhoea, and no blood in the stool. On examination she is alert and interactive but quiet, with pale conjunctivae and no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising and a normal neurological examination with no focal deficit and a normal gait. Her weight and length have tracked along the 25th centile throughout.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, abdomen soft with palpable faecal loading, no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, normal tone gait and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 66 fL (73-85), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-150), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), platelets 288 x10^9/L (150-450), basophilic stippling noted on the film

lead_in: Which investigation should you request to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Venous blood lead level, taken with attention to avoiding external contamination
options.rationale: Residence near a smelter, a renovated pre-1970 house, a history of putting things in the mouth at this age, developmental regression, abdominal pain and a microcytic anaemia with stippled red cells together make lead the unifying explanation, and a venous level is the test that confirms it. Capillary samples are prone to skin contamination and a raised result on a finger prick still requires venous confirmation. (Source: NHMRC Information Paper: Evidence on the effects of lead on human health)
source_refs: NHMRC Information Paper: Evidence on the effects of lead on human health

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to look for marrow infiltration or failure
options.rationale: Marrow examination is indicated when an anaemia is accompanied by abnormal white cells or platelets, blasts on the film, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy or bone pain, and all of those are absent here. An isolated microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin is a peripheral problem, not a marrow one. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Anaemia

options.text: Urinary catecholamines with an abdominal ultrasound looking for a solid tumour
options.rationale: Neuroblastoma can present with irritability, anaemia and loss of milestones, but it almost always produces a mass, bone pain, periorbital bruising or hepatomegaly, none of which are found. The environmental history and basophilic stippling point away from malignancy. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass

options.text: Haemoglobin electrophoresis with iron studies to separate thalassaemia from deficiency
options.rationale: Electrophoresis is the right test when a microcytosis is disproportionate to the anaemia and iron stores are normal, whereas this child's ferritin of 9 micrograms/L already shows genuine iron deficiency. Neither result would account for the language regression or the stippled film. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Anaemia

options.text: Coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A on a normal gluten containing diet
options.rationale: Coeliac disease is a fair explanation for iron deficiency with abdominal pain, but it does not cause loss of acquired speech, and it produces loose stools or faltering growth rather than constipation with centile-stable growth. It remains a reasonable second line test if lead is not the answer. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease

explanation.summary: Chronic lead exposure in Australian children clusters around smelter towns such as Port Pirie, Broken Hill and Mount Isa, and around disturbed pre-1970 lead paint during renovation. The presentation is deliberately non-specific: colicky abdominal pain, constipation, irritability and loss of language milestones, with a microcytic anaemia that is worsened by coexisting iron deficiency because low iron increases lead absorption. Basophilic stippling is suggestive but neither sensitive nor specific, so the diagnosis rests on a venous blood lead level. Management is source removal and iron repletion, with chelation reserved for high levels or encephalopathy, and notification thresholds follow the national guidance.
key_points: Ask about smelter towns, pre-1970 housing and recent renovation in any child with unexplained regression
Iron deficiency increases gut absorption of lead, so the two commonly coexist and each worsens the other
A venous sample is required because capillary samples are contaminated by skin lead
Source removal and iron repletion come first, with chelation reserved for very high levels or encephalopathy
explanation.pearls: In an Australian toddler with a microcytic anaemia and lost words, the exposure history is the test-selector: a house built before 1970 that has been sanded or stripped, or an address in a smelter town, should trigger a venous blood lead level, and a level at or above 5 micrograms per decilitre is the national threshold for investigating and removing the source rather than simply treating the iron deficiency.

subtopic_detail: scaly scalp patch with broken hairs and occipital lymph nodes unresponsive to topical antifungal cream
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy whose mother has been treating a patch on his scalp for six weeks. She has used a topical clotrimazole cream from the pharmacy twice daily throughout, and the patch has slowly enlarged.

On examination there is a 4 cm round scaly patch over the left occiput with hairs broken off a few millimetres above the skin, and a few small mobile lymph nodes at the occiput on the same side. The scalp is not boggy, there is no pus, no crusted honey coloured exudate and no fluctuance. He is systemically well and afebrile, and the rest of his skin and his nails are normal. A skin scraping and plucked hairs have been sent for fungal microscopy and culture, with results expected in three weeks.

data_table.Examination: Round scaly occipital patch with hairs broken close to the scalp, ipsilateral occipital lymphadenopathy, no boggy swelling or pustules
data_table.Treatment to date: Topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for six weeks with progressive enlargement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start oral griseofulvin daily with fatty food and continue it for six to eight weeks
options.rationale: Fungal infection of the scalp involves the hair shaft and follicle, which topical agents cannot penetrate, so oral therapy is required and treatment is started before culture returns when the clinical picture is characteristic. Griseofulvin with a fatty meal to aid absorption remains a standard first line oral agent for this infection in children. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections

options.text: Switch to ketoconazole shampoo twice weekly and review the patch in one month
options.rationale: Antifungal shampoo reduces surface spore shedding and is a useful adjunct that limits spread to classmates and siblings, but it does not reach the fungus inside the hair shaft and will not cure the infection. Using it alone repeats the error of the last six weeks with a different bottle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to treat bacterial infection of the hair follicles
options.rationale: Antibiotics would be needed for a boggy pustular inflammatory mass with secondary bacterial infection, but there is no fluctuance, no pus and no systemic upset here. Treating a dermatophyte with cefalexin lets the scarring alopecia progress untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment daily to settle the inflamed scaly patch
options.rationale: A corticosteroid would be the treatment if this were scalp psoriasis or discoid eczema, but those do not break hairs off at the scalp or produce regional lymphadenopathy. Steroid applied to an untreated dermatophyte suppresses the inflammation while the fungus spreads. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections

options.text: Wait for the fungal culture before starting any systemic treatment, and keep him home
options.rationale: Culture takes up to four weeks and guides the choice of agent and duration, but withholding treatment during that wait allows further hair loss and ongoing transmission. Australian practice is to treat on the clinical picture and adjust once the organism is known, and exclusion from school is not required once treatment has begun. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections

explanation.summary: Scalp dermatophyte infection is distinguished from other scaly scalp conditions by hairs broken close to the skin and by regional lymphadenopathy, which are absent in psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis. Because the organism lives within the hair shaft, topical antifungals cannot cure it, and six weeks of a topical cream that has failed is itself part of the pattern. Oral therapy with griseofulvin or terbinafine is started on clinical grounds while culture is pending, with an antifungal shampoo added to reduce shedding and household spread. Untreated infection can progress to a boggy inflammatory mass with permanent scarring alopecia.
key_points: Hairs broken at the scalp surface plus occipital lymph nodes are the clinical signature of scalp dermatophytosis
Topical antifungals fail because the organism is inside the hair shaft
Start oral therapy on clinical grounds; culture refines the agent and duration later
Antifungal shampoo is an adjunct to reduce spore shedding, never the sole treatment
explanation.pearls: Feel for occipital nodes whenever you assess a scaly scalp in a child: their presence alongside hairs broken a few millimetres above the skin makes dermatophyte infection likely enough to start oral griseofulvin the same day, typically for six to eight weeks and given with a fatty meal, rather than waiting the three to four weeks that culture takes.

subtopic_detail: thick fissured hyperkeratotic crusts on palms and soles in a child from a remote community with little itch
stem:
You are the doctor at a remote community clinic in the Northern Territory. A 7-year-old girl is brought in with thick grey crusted plaques on both palms and soles that have built up over several months, with deep painful fissures. Her scalp and back have thick scale as well.

Her grandmother says the girl barely scratches, which is why nobody thought it was the same thing her cousins had. Two other children in the household have an itchy papular rash between the fingers and on the wrists. This girl was treated for nephrotic syndrome last year and is taking prednisolone. She is systemically well, afebrile, with no cellulitis, no discharging sores and no joint swelling. Skin scrapings taken today are reported within the hour as showing numerous mites and eggs.

data_table.Examination: Thick grey hyperkeratotic fissured crusts on palms, soles and scalp, minimal excoriation, no cellulitis or purulent sores
data_table.Household: Two other children with an itchy papular eruption of the finger webs and wrists
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone, ongoing since treatment for nephrotic syndrome last year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: A single dose of oral ivermectin today, repeated once in seven days, for this child only
options.rationale: Two doses is the regimen for ordinary scabies, but a heavily crusted infestation carries millions of mites and requires multiple ivermectin doses combined with a topical agent and keratolytic therapy. Treating only the index child also leaves the household reservoir untouched. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies)
source_refs: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies

options.text: Topical permethrin 5% cream applied once tonight and repeated after one week
options.rationale: Permethrin alone cannot penetrate crusts that are millimetres thick, so mites survive in the deeper layers and the child relapses. It remains part of the regimen, but only alongside keratolytic softening and repeated oral ivermectin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Scabies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Scabies

options.text: Multi-dose oral ivermectin with topical permethrin and keratolytic, plus household treatment
options.rationale: Crusted infestation is treated as a combination protocol because the crust shelters an enormous mite burden: a keratolytic such as urea or salicylic acid softens the scale, topical scabicide is applied to the softened skin, and oral ivermectin is repeated on a schedule determined by severity. Simultaneous treatment of every household contact prevents the immediate reinfestation that otherwise follows. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies)
source_refs: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies

options.text: Oral cefalexin for ten days with daily bleach baths and dressings to the fissures
options.rationale: Antibiotics are added when there is impetigo or cellulitis complicating the infestation, and that matters in this setting because of the risk of subsequent acute rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. There is no pus or cellulitis described, and antibiotics do nothing about the mite burden. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections)
source_refs: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections

options.text: Cease prednisolone immediately and review the skin in one week before treating the mites
options.rationale: Immune suppression is the reason the infestation became crusted and the steroid dose should be reviewed with her nephrology team, but abrupt cessation risks adrenal insufficiency and relapse of the underlying renal disease. The infestation is treated now, not after a week of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome

explanation.summary: Crusted scabies is the hyperinfested form seen in immune suppression, and the diagnostic trap is that itch is minimal or absent, so the appearance is mistaken for eczema or psoriasis. Thick fissured plaques on palms, soles and scalp in a child on prednisolone, with classic burrow rash in other household members, is the recognisable pattern. Because the crust shelters an extremely high mite burden, single-agent treatment fails: the regimen combines a keratolytic to soften scale, topical permethrin, and repeated doses of oral ivermectin, with simultaneous treatment of all contacts. In northern and central Australia this is also a public health matter, since the associated streptococcal skin infection drives acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and acute rheumatic fever.
key_points: Minimal itch does not exclude scabies and is characteristic of the crusted form
Thick crusts shelter mites from topical agents, so keratolytic softening is part of treatment
Repeated oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide is the standard combination for crusted disease
Treat every household contact at the same time or reinfestation is immediate
explanation.pearls: When a child on immunosuppression has thick crusted plaques and does not scratch, ask what rash the other children in the house have: classic finger web itch in contacts alongside minimal itch in the index case is crusted scabies, and it needs a keratolytic plus topical permethrin plus a multi-dose oral ivermectin schedule with same-day treatment of the whole household.

sources.label: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies
CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections

subtopic_detail: clockwork monthly fevers with aphthous ulcers and pharyngitis and complete wellness between episodes
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar in a fever clinic. A 4-year-old boy has had fevers to 39.5 degrees Celsius every four weeks for the past eight months. Each episode lasts four days and his mother can predict the next one on the calendar.

During episodes he has mouth ulcers, a sore throat and tender neck glands, and he looks miserable but is never admitted. Between episodes he is entirely well, attends kindergarten, and his weight and height have tracked steadily along the 50th centile. Two throat swabs taken during previous episodes grew normal flora, and a full blood count during a well period was normal. He has received all scheduled immunisations, has had no rash, no joint swelling, no abdominal pain and no diarrhoea, and there has been no overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile and well today, all vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination during episodes: Temperature to 39.5 degrees Celsius, aphthous oral ulcers, exudative pharyngitis, tender cervical lymph nodes
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count during a well interval normal, two throat swabs during episodes grew normal flora, growth along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for the next episode?

options.text: Prescribe oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for ten days at the start of the next episode
options.rationale: Penicillin treats streptococcal pharyngitis, which would produce positive swabs and a course that does not recur on a monthly timetable. Repeated antibiotic courses for this pattern expose the child without altering the interval. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis

options.text: Arrange genetic testing for familial Mediterranean fever before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Monogenic periodic fever syndromes are considered when episodes involve serositis, rash, arthritis or amyloidosis, or when there is a suggestive ethnic and family history, and their attacks are not calendar-regular. Testing is reasonable if the course deviates, but it should not delay a therapeutic step that is also diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes

options.text: Admit during the next episode for bone marrow examination and a whole body scan
options.rationale: Malignancy is the concern behind recurrent fever, but it produces progressive illness, faltering growth, cytopenias or organomegaly rather than eight months of complete wellness between identical four-day episodes. Invasive investigation is not justified by this pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Fever without focus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fever without focus

options.text: Give a single dose of oral prednisolone at the onset of fever and record the response
options.rationale: A single corticosteroid dose given as the fever starts typically aborts the episode within hours in this syndrome, which makes it both the treatment and a strong diagnostic confirmation. Families are counselled that steroid may shorten the interval between episodes, and that the condition is self limiting over years with normal growth throughout. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes

options.text: Refer for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy as the definitive treatment for the syndrome
options.rationale: Tonsillectomy does resolve this syndrome in many children and is a recognised option, but it is a second line consideration for frequent disabling episodes after the diagnosis has been established and the natural resolution explained. Proceeding to surgery before a steroid trial skips the least invasive confirmatory step. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes

explanation.summary: Periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and cervical adenitis is the commonest periodic fever syndrome of early childhood and is defined clinically by its regularity. The three features that make the diagnosis are clockwork recurrence, complete wellness between episodes, and entirely normal growth. Negative throat swabs and a normal interval blood count exclude the alternatives that would otherwise need treatment. A single dose of prednisolone at fever onset usually aborts the attack within hours, which both treats the episode and confirms the diagnosis, although families should be warned that episodes may then recur sooner.
key_points: Calendar regularity with complete wellness between episodes is the diagnostic hallmark
Normal growth and a normal interval blood count argue against malignancy and immunodeficiency
A single dose of prednisolone at fever onset usually aborts the episode within hours
Steroid may shorten the interval between attacks; tonsillectomy is a later option for disabling disease
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to bring the calendar or phone diary: fevers that fall every three to six weeks to the day, each lasting three to five days with mouth ulcers and a sore throat, with a completely well child in between and a normal growth chart, is periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and adenitis, and a single prednisolone dose at onset that aborts the fever within hours seals the diagnosis without any genetic test.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes

Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis

subtopic_detail: choosing seasonal immunisation for a preterm infant approaching their first winter with a well sibling at school
stem:
You are the doctor running a general practice baby clinic in early autumn. A 3-month-old boy born at 32 weeks gestation attends for his scheduled immunisations. He was in the special care nursery for three weeks with no chronic lung disease and has been well since discharge, feeding and growing along the 25th centile.

His mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy but says she was not offered any vaccines during it and received none. His 4-year-old sister is well and fully immunised. There is no family history of immunodeficiency, and the baby has had no wheeze, no admissions and no oxygen requirement since going home. His mother is worried because a neighbour's baby was admitted to intensive care last winter with a chest infection, and she asks what can be done to protect him through the coming season.

data_table.History: Born at 32 weeks, three weeks in special care, no chronic lung disease, no oxygen at home
data_table.Growth: Weight tracking the 25th centile since discharge

lead_in: In addition to his scheduled vaccines, what should you recommend today?

options.text: Palivizumab given monthly through the winter season to this infant only
options.rationale: Monthly injections are burdensome and this product has largely been replaced in Australian programs by a single dose long acting monoclonal antibody covering a whole season. Monthly dosing also restricted eligibility to the most severe chronic lung and cardiac disease, which this infant does not have. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.text: A single dose of nirsevimab before the season, since his mother was not vaccinated
options.rationale: Protection against respiratory syncytial virus in the first season comes either from maternal vaccination in pregnancy or from a long acting monoclonal antibody given to the infant, and this mother received neither, so the infant needs the antibody. A single dose before or early in the season covers approximately five months, and prematurity places him in the group that benefits most. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.text: Influenza vaccine for the infant now, with a second dose given four weeks later
options.rationale: Influenza vaccine is recommended from 6 months of age, with two doses in the first year of vaccination, so it is a real part of this family's winter plan but cannot be given at 3 months. Cocooning by vaccinating the household is the interim measure at this age. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Influenza)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Influenza

options.text: Defer all additional protection until 6 months of corrected age and review then
options.rationale: Correcting for prematurity is right for developmental milestones but wrong for immunisation, which follows chronological age, and deferral would leave him unprotected through the very season in question. Preterm infants are at higher risk of severe bronchiolitis, not lower. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants

options.text: Vaccinate the mother against respiratory syncytial virus now so her milk protects him
options.rationale: Maternal vaccination works by transferring antibody across the placenta in the third trimester, so giving it after birth does not protect an infant already born. Breast milk carries some protection but not the specific antibody titre this strategy relies on. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

explanation.summary: Protection of infants against respiratory syncytial virus in their first winter now runs along two alternative routes: maternal vaccination in the third trimester, or a long acting monoclonal antibody given directly to the infant. When the mother was not vaccinated during pregnancy the infant route applies, and nirsevimab is given as a single dose before or early in the season to cover roughly five months. Preterm birth increases the risk of severe bronchiolitis and strengthens the indication, while immunisation itself follows chronological rather than corrected age. Influenza vaccine remains part of the winter plan from 6 months of age, with household cocooning until then.
key_points: Either maternal third trimester vaccination or infant monoclonal antibody protects the first season, not both routes by default
Maternal vaccine given after delivery does not protect the infant, since the mechanism is transplacental antibody
Scheduled vaccines for preterm infants follow chronological age, not corrected age
Influenza vaccine starts at 6 months, with two doses in the first year of vaccination
explanation.pearls: For any infant facing their first winter, ask one question first: did the mother receive a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine in the third trimester? If not, the infant needs a single dose of nirsevimab before or early in the season, and the dose is scheduled by chronological age even in a baby born at 32 weeks.

sources.label: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus
Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants
Australian Immunisation Handbook: Influenza

subtopic_detail: asymptomatic hip migration on surveillance imaging in a non-ambulant child with bilateral spasticity
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric rehabilitation clinic. A 5-year-old girl with bilateral spastic cerebral palsy attends for review. She has never walked and uses a supportive seating system, which corresponds to level four on the standard functional classification.

Her parents report no pain at all, and she tolerates sitting, standing frame sessions and nappy changes without distress. On examination hip abduction in flexion is 35 degrees on the right and 30 degrees on the left, with no fixed flexion contracture and no leg length discrepancy. A surveillance anteroposterior pelvic radiograph performed this month is reported with a migration percentage of 38 per cent on the right and 34 per cent on the left. The films from 12 months ago showed 24 per cent and 22 per cent. She has no scoliosis and her seating has not changed.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral spasticity, hip abduction in flexion 35 degrees right and 30 degrees left, no pain on hip movement, no fixed contracture
data_table.Imaging: Migration percentage right 38 per cent and left 34 per cent, compared with 24 per cent and 22 per cent 12 months ago
data_table.Function: Non-ambulant, supportive seating, level four on the gross motor functional classification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the pelvic radiograph in 12 months as part of routine surveillance imaging
options.rationale: Annual imaging is the correct interval for a stable hip in a child at this functional level, but a migration percentage that has risen by 14 points in a year and crossed 30 per cent has already breached the threshold for referral. Continuing to watch risks silent progression to dislocation and later pain. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Prescribe regular oral baclofen and review the hip clinically in three months
options.rationale: Tone reduction is a useful adjunct that can improve comfort and ease of care, but no medical therapy reverses established femoral head displacement. Relying on baclofen would let the migration percentage keep climbing while the window for simpler surgery closes. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Reassure the family that intervention is unnecessary while the hips remain pain free
options.rationale: Displacement in this population is characteristically painless until the hip is subluxed or dislocated, which is precisely why radiographic surveillance exists rather than symptom-triggered imaging. Waiting for pain means intervening after the deformity is established. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics now given the migration percentage and its rate of change
options.rationale: A migration percentage above 30 per cent, or a rise of more than 10 percentage points in a year, is the trigger for orthopaedic referral regardless of symptoms, and both criteria are met here. Early referral allows soft tissue surgery or preventive reconstruction before the head displaces far enough to require salvage procedures. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Arrange botulinum toxin injections to the hip adductors as the definitive management
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin can improve adductor tone and sitting comfort and may be used alongside surgical planning, but it has not been shown to prevent progressive displacement on its own. Offering it as the definitive answer substitutes a temporary tone measure for the structural assessment the imaging demands. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

explanation.summary: Hip displacement in cerebral palsy is progressive, painless in its early stages, and closely related to gross motor function, which is why Australian practice uses scheduled radiographic surveillance rather than waiting for symptoms. The measurement that drives decisions is the migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying lateral to the lateral margin of the acetabulum. Referral to orthopaedics is triggered by a migration percentage above 30 per cent or a rise of more than 10 percentage points between annual films, and this child meets both. Tone management with baclofen or botulinum toxin supports comfort and care but does not reverse established displacement.
key_points: Surveillance frequency is set by gross motor function level, and non-ambulant children carry the highest risk
Migration percentage above 30 per cent triggers orthopaedic referral even in a pain free child
A rise of more than 10 percentage points in a year is itself a referral trigger
Tone reduction improves comfort and care but does not prevent progressive displacement
explanation.pearls: Compare the migration percentage with the previous film rather than reading it in isolation: in a non-ambulant child with cerebral palsy, either crossing 30 per cent or gaining more than 10 percentage points in a year warrants orthopaedic referral that day, because these hips are painless until they are already subluxed.

sources.label: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy
RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy

subtopic_detail: painless ear discharge through a persistent drum perforation for more than six weeks in a remote community child
stem:
You are the doctor at a remote community clinic. A 5-year-old boy is brought in because his right ear has been running for three months. His grandmother says it never hurts him and he never has fever with it, but she has to wipe it most days.

On otoscopy, after you dry the canal with rolled tissue spears, there is a large central perforation of the right tympanic membrane with mucoid discharge coming through it. The canal skin is not swollen and the pinna is not tender to move. The left drum is dull and retracted but intact. He has no facial weakness, no swelling behind the ear, no headache and no neck stiffness, and he is systemically well. His school teacher has reported that he does not respond when called from across the room and has fallen behind with reading.

data_table.Examination: Large central right tympanic membrane perforation with mucoid discharge, non-tender pinna and mastoid, left drum dull and retracted
data_table.Duration: Discharge continuous for three months, painless, no fever
data_table.Function: Teacher reports poor response to speech across the classroom and falling behind with reading

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin for seven days with review at the clinic once the course is finished
options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin is the treatment for acute otitis media with an intact drum and systemic symptoms, a picture that includes pain and fever rather than three painless months of discharge. Once a perforation is chronically discharging, oral therapy alone rarely dries the ear because the biofilm sits in the middle ear cleft. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.text: Framycetin with gramicidin and dexamethasone ear drops applied three times daily
options.rationale: This combination is used for infection of the canal skin where the drum is intact, and the aminoglycoside component is avoided when the middle ear is open because of the risk of inner ear toxicity. The non-tender pinna and normal canal skin indicate the problem is not an outer ear infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Otitis media

options.text: Urgent transfer for intravenous antibiotics and a computed tomography scan of the mastoid
options.rationale: Urgent imaging and admission are for suspected intracranial or mastoid complications, signalled by fever, postauricular swelling, facial nerve palsy, severe headache or vertigo, and none of these are present. Transferring a systemically well child out of community for a chronic problem delays the treatment that actually helps. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.text: Refer for grommet insertion into both ears at the next visiting surgical outreach clinic
options.rationale: A ventilation tube is used for persistent middle ear fluid behind an intact drum, and the right ear is already ventilated by the perforation itself, so a tube adds nothing there. Surgical repair of the drum is considered only after the ear has been dry for a prolonged period and the child is older. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.text: Dry mopping with topical ciprofloxacin drops and referral for formal audiology assessment
options.rationale: Discharge through a perforation lasting beyond six weeks is treated by regular cleaning of the canal so that drops reach the middle ear, together with a quinolone preparation that is not toxic to the inner ear when the drum is open. Audiology is mandatory rather than optional because the hearing loss is driving the classroom difficulty and needs measurement and amplification planning. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

explanation.summary: Painless discharge through a perforation persisting beyond six weeks defines chronic suppurative otitis media, which carries a high burden in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and is a leading cause of preventable childhood hearing loss in Australia. The treatment that changes outcomes is mechanical: dry mopping the canal so that topical antibiotic actually reaches the middle ear, using a quinolone because aminoglycoside drops risk cochlear toxicity through an open drum. Systemic antibiotics have a limited role unless there are signs of complication such as mastoiditis or facial palsy. Audiology referral is an essential part of the plan, since the conductive loss affects language and schooling and may need amplification or classroom sound field support.
key_points: Discharge through a perforation beyond six weeks is chronic, not acute, otitis media
Dry mopping before drops is what allows topical therapy to reach the middle ear
Use quinolone drops rather than aminoglycoside preparations when the drum is perforated
Every child with chronic discharge needs audiology and educational support, not antibiotics alone
explanation.pearls: Treat the hearing as seriously as the discharge: a child with a chronically discharging ear who does not answer when called across a classroom needs formal audiology and school based amplification alongside dry mopping and ciprofloxacin drops, because the conductive loss rather than the infection is what costs them their reading.

sources.label: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Otitis media
RCH CPG: Acute otitis media

subtopic_detail: breast development in a tall adolescent boy whose testes remain small despite advanced pubic hair
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 14-year-old boy brought by his father because of breast development that has not settled over the past 18 months. He avoids swimming because of it.

His height is above the 97th centile although both parents are of average height, and his arm span exceeds his height by 7 cm. Pubic hair is well developed, but on examination both testes measure 4 mL by orchidometer and are firm. He has symmetrical soft breast tissue with no discrete mass, no nipple discharge, and no skin change. He takes no regular medications, no supplements and no anabolic agents, and he does not use cannabis. He needed extra help with reading in primary school and still finds written work hard. There is no abdominal mass and no hepatomegaly, and the rest of the examination is normal.

data_table.Examination: Height above 97th centile, arm span exceeding height by 7 cm, bilateral symmetrical breast tissue, testes 4 mL and firm, advanced pubic hair
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), beta human chorionic gonadotropin less than 2 IU/L, morning testosterone low for age with raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone
data_table.Medications: None, including no supplements or anabolic agents

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Testicular ultrasound looking for a hormone secreting germ cell or Leydig cell tumour
options.rationale: A hormonally active testicular tumour is the concern when gynaecomastia is accompanied by a palpable testicular mass or a raised beta human chorionic gonadotropin, and both are absent here. Bilateral small firm testes point to failure of the gonad rather than a tumour within it. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary to exclude a prolactin secreting adenoma
options.rationale: A pituitary lesion causing hypogonadism would suppress rather than elevate the gonadotropins, so the raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone place the lesion below the pituitary. Imaging the pituitary here would be normal and would delay the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia

options.text: Repeat clinical review in six months, since pubertal breast tissue usually resolves by then
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for physiological pubertal gynaecomastia, which occurs at mid puberty with normally enlarging testes of 10 mL or more and resolves within two years. Testes of 4 mL alongside advanced pubic hair is a mismatch that excludes the physiological pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia

options.text: Urine drug screen for anabolic androgenic steroids and other exogenous hormone exposure
options.rationale: Exogenous androgen use suppresses the gonadotropins and shrinks the testes, so it belongs in the differential of small testes with gynaecomastia, but the raised gonadotropins here point the other way. The history of no supplement or anabolic use is consistent with that biochemistry. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia

options.text: Karyotype analysis on a peripheral blood sample to define the underlying chromosomal pattern
options.rationale: Small firm testes with a raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone identify primary testicular failure, and in a tall adolescent with disproportionately long limbs, breast development and learning difficulty the explanation is an additional X chromosome. Karyotype confirms it and opens the discussion about testosterone replacement and fertility preservation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia

explanation.summary: The discriminating finding in adolescent gynaecomastia is testicular volume interpreted against the stage of pubic hair. Physiological pubertal gynaecomastia occurs when the testes are already 10 mL or larger and settles within about two years, whereas testes of 4 mL with advanced pubic hair indicates that androgen is coming from the adrenal while the testis has failed. A raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone localises the problem to the gonad, and the combination with tall stature, long limbs and learning difficulties is characteristic of an additional X chromosome. Karyotype confirms the diagnosis, after which management involves paediatric endocrinology, testosterone replacement, educational support and early counselling about fertility.
key_points: Measure testicular volume with an orchidometer before attributing gynaecomastia to puberty
Raised gonadotropins localise the defect to the testis rather than the pituitary
Tall stature with long limbs and learning difficulty alongside small firm testes suggests an extra X chromosome
Suppressed gonadotropins with small testes would instead suggest exogenous androgen use
explanation.pearls: Gynaecomastia plus testes under 6 mL in a boy with well developed pubic hair is never physiological: check morning testosterone with luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone, and if the gonadotropins are high, send a karyotype rather than scheduling a six month review.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia
Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Delayed puberty and hypogonadism

subtopic_detail: overdue routine cervical screening in a woman who declines a speculum examination after past trauma
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 32-year-old woman attends for a repeat prescription and mentions she has never had a cervical screening test. She is now seven years past the age at which screening should have started.

She has no abnormal bleeding, no bleeding after intercourse, no unusual discharge and no pelvic pain. She has had two normal vaginal births and no gynaecological surgery. She tells you that she experienced sexual assault in her twenties and that the thought of a speculum examination is the reason she has avoided screening, and she becomes tearful describing this. She is not pregnant, uses a hormonal implant for contraception, and is otherwise well with a normal examination of the abdomen. She asks whether there is any way to be screened that does not involve an internal examination.

data_table.History: Never screened, seven years overdue, two normal vaginal births, hormonal implant in situ
data_table.Symptoms: No abnormal or postcoital bleeding, no discharge, no pelvic pain
data_table.Barriers: Declines speculum examination following past sexual assault

lead_in: What should you offer her?

options.text: A self-collected vaginal swab for human papillomavirus testing taken today in the practice
options.rationale: Self-collection is available to every person eligible for routine cervical screening, not only to those who have declined repeatedly, and it detects the virus with accuracy equivalent to a clinician-collected sample. It converts a seven year gap into a completed screen at this visit, with follow up determined by whether the virus is detected and which type. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: Referral to a gynaecologist for screening under general anaesthesia at a day surgery unit
options.rationale: Examination under anaesthesia is reserved for situations where an adequate assessment is impossible awake and where a diagnostic procedure such as colposcopy or biopsy is genuinely required. Using it for routine screening exposes a well woman to anaesthetic risk when a swab she takes herself achieves the same result. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: A blood test for human papillomavirus antibodies as an alternative to any genital sampling
options.rationale: Serology reflects past exposure rather than current cervical infection and has no role in any national screening program. Offering it would give a result that cannot be interpreted against screening pathways. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: Deferral of screening with review in twelve months once she has completed trauma counselling
options.rationale: Trauma informed care and counselling are valuable and should be offered, but deferring adds another year to a seven year gap when an acceptable test is available immediately. Support and screening are not alternatives to each other. (Source: RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

options.text: A liquid based cervical cytology sample collected by a female clinician using a small speculum
options.rationale: Cytology is no longer the primary screening test in Australia, having been replaced by primary testing for the virus at five yearly intervals, and cytology is now performed reflexively on a positive sample. Offering a smaller speculum and a female clinician is good practice but still requires the internal examination she has declined. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

explanation.summary: Australian cervical screening is now primary testing for human papillomavirus every five years from age 25 until 74, and self-collection is a universally available option rather than a concession for the reluctant. A self-collected vaginal sample performs equivalently to a clinician-collected sample for the detection of oncogenic types, which is what makes it acceptable for routine screening. Management follows the result: types 16 or 18 lead directly to colposcopy, while other oncogenic types trigger reflex cytology on the same sample, which for a self-collected specimen requires a subsequent clinician-collected sample. For a woman whose barrier to screening is a history of sexual assault, offering self-collection is both trauma informed and clinically complete.
key_points: Primary human papillomavirus testing every five years replaced two yearly cytology in Australia
Self-collection is offered to all eligible people and performs equivalently for oncogenic type detection
Detection of type 16 or 18 leads directly to colposcopy regardless of how the sample was taken
Other oncogenic types trigger reflex cytology, which needs a clinician-collected sample if self-collection was used
explanation.pearls: When a patient names the speculum as the barrier, the screen can still be completed that day: a self-collected vaginal swab for human papillomavirus is equivalent for detecting oncogenic types, and only if a type other than 16 or 18 is found does she need to return for a clinician-collected sample for reflex cytology.

subtopic_detail: request for emergency contraception three days after unprotected sex with a high body mass index and no ongoing method
stem:
You are the doctor in a walk-in sexual health clinic. A 24-year-old woman attends asking for the morning after pill. Unprotected intercourse occurred 72 hours ago and again 20 hours ago.

Her last menstrual period began 12 days ago and her cycles are regular at 28 days. Her body mass index is 38 kg/m2 and she weighs 104 kg. She has no contraception at present, having stopped the combined pill two years ago, and tells you she does not want to become pregnant and would like something long term so that she is not in this position again. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease, no abnormal bleeding, and a negative urine pregnancy test today. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea swabs have been taken. She has no known allergies and takes no regular medications, including no enzyme inducing drugs.

data_table.History: Unprotected intercourse 72 hours and 20 hours ago, day 12 of a regular 28 day cycle
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg/m2, weight 104 kg, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, sexually transmitted infection swabs taken today

lead_in: What is the most effective option to offer her?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally now, with a double dose given because of her body weight
options.rationale: Oral levonorgestrel loses efficacy with increasing body weight and is also less effective than the alternatives beyond 72 hours, and doubling the dose has not been shown to restore effectiveness reliably. It remains a reasonable option when a device is declined or unavailable, but it is not the most effective choice here. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device at this visit with swab results followed up
options.rationale: A copper device inserted within five days of the earliest unprotected act is the most effective emergency method, with a failure rate well under one per cent, and its efficacy is unaffected by body weight. It simultaneously provides the long term contraception she is asking for, and screening swabs can be treated if positive without removing the device. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally now, followed by an etonogestrel implant inserted today
options.rationale: Ulipristal works closer to ovulation than levonorgestrel but is also less reliable at higher body weight, and inserting a progestogen implant immediately afterwards reduces its effectiveness because the progestogen opposes its action. If ulipristal is used, progestogen contraception is delayed for five days. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: A hormonal intrauterine device inserted today, which also treats heavy menstrual bleeding
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel releasing device is excellent ongoing contraception but has not been established as emergency contraception in Australian guidance, since its mechanism does not reliably prevent implantation after an act that has already occurred. Choosing it here would leave this cycle unprotected. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Reassurance that pregnancy is unlikely, with a pregnancy test repeated in three weeks
options.rationale: Day 12 of a 28 day cycle sits within the fertile window immediately before ovulation, which is the period of highest conception risk rather than the lowest. Deferring to a later pregnancy test abandons an intervention that is still available within the five day window. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

explanation.summary: The copper intrauterine device is the most effective form of emergency contraception, works up to five days after the earliest unprotected act or up to five days after the estimated day of ovulation, and unlike the oral options is not affected by body weight. That weight independence matters here because both levonorgestrel and ulipristal show reduced efficacy at higher body mass index. Fitting the device also answers her request for ongoing contraception in one visit, and a positive chlamydia or gonorrhoea result can be treated with the device left in place. Oral options remain appropriate when a device is declined, unavailable, or when insertion would delay treatment past the window.
key_points: A copper device is the most effective emergency method and is unaffected by body weight
Insertion is possible up to five days after the earliest unprotected act
Levonorgestrel and ulipristal both lose efficacy at higher body mass index
Starting a progestogen method within five days of ulipristal reduces the effectiveness of the ulipristal
explanation.pearls: In a woman over 70 kg or with a body mass index above 30 who needs emergency contraception, lead with the copper intrauterine device: its efficacy does not fall with body weight, it covers up to five days from the earliest act, and it converts the visit into ongoing long acting contraception.
