RANZCOG: Emergency contraception

subtopic_detail: counselling about skeletal effects for an adolescent who has used a three monthly injectable for two years
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 17-year-old woman who has used three monthly depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injections for two years. She is amenorrhoeic on it, is delighted with the method, and asks to continue.

She has intellectual disability and, with her mother, describes how difficult daily tablets were before the injections. Her weight is stable, she eats a varied diet, spends time outdoors most days and plays in a netball team. She has no fractures, no chronic illness, takes no corticosteroids or anticonvulsants, and has never had an eating disorder. Her mother has read online that the injection weakens bones permanently and asks whether it must be stopped at the two year mark. There is no family history of osteoporosis or early fracture, and her mother is 50 with no fracture history.

data_table.History: Two years of continuous three monthly injections, amenorrhoeic, no fractures
data_table.Risk factors: No corticosteroids or anticonvulsants, no eating disorder, weight bearing sport most weeks, stable weight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: She should stop at two years because the skeletal loss becomes irreversible after that point
options.rationale: A fixed two year ceiling was based on an early regulatory warning, and subsequent evidence shows that density recovers after discontinuation, including in adolescents. Enforcing an arbitrary stop date risks an unintended pregnancy in someone for whom other methods have already failed. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: She should have a bone density scan now, with the result deciding whether to continue
options.rationale: Scanning is not recommended for routine monitoring of this method because interpretation in a still-growing skeleton is difficult and there is no threshold that guides contraceptive decisions. It is reserved for those with additional risks such as prolonged corticosteroid use, an eating disorder or prior fragility fracture. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: She may continue it, with the benefits and alternatives reviewed at each repeat injection
options.rationale: Bone mineral density falls modestly during use and recovers substantially after stopping, so Australian guidance sets no absolute duration limit and instead calls for periodic review of whether the method still suits the person. For an adolescent whose adherence to daily methods has failed, the pregnancy risk of switching outweighs a reversible density change. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: She should switch to a combined oral contraceptive to protect bone with added oestrogen
options.rationale: Adding oestrogen has not been shown to be necessary for bone in healthy users, and moving to a daily tablet reintroduces exactly the adherence problem that prompted the injection. A daily method is the wrong direction for someone who struggled with tablets. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: She should start a bisphosphonate alongside the injection to prevent further loss of bone
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates treat established osteoporosis or high fracture risk, neither of which applies to a healthy adolescent with no fractures, and they persist in bone for years with uncertain implications for future pregnancy. Prescribing one here creates risk rather than removing it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Osteoporosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Osteoporosis

explanation.summary: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate suppresses ovarian oestrogen production and produces a modest reduction in bone mineral density during use, which largely recovers after discontinuation, including when started in adolescence. Australian guidance therefore places no fixed limit on duration and asks instead for a periodic review of benefits, alternatives and individual risk factors at each injection. Routine bone densitometry is not recommended because there is no density threshold that guides contraceptive choice in this group, and it is difficult to interpret before peak bone mass is reached. Additional caution applies to those with prolonged corticosteroid use, an eating disorder, prior fragility fracture or other causes of low bone density.
key_points: Density loss during use is modest and substantially reversible after discontinuation
No arbitrary two year stopping rule applies in current Australian guidance
Routine bone densitometry is not recommended for monitoring this method
Review at each injection covers benefits, alternatives and individual risk factors
explanation.pearls: Weigh the reversible density change against the actual alternative for this person: in an adolescent whose daily pill adherence failed, continuing the injection with a documented benefit-and-alternatives conversation every three months is supported, and bone densitometry is added only when there is corticosteroid use, an eating disorder or a previous fragility fracture.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Osteoporosis
RANZCOG: Long acting reversible contraception

subtopic_detail: heavy regular periods with a normal pelvis in a woman who wants to conceive within a few months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 34-year-old woman describes periods that soak through a pad every hour on her two heaviest days and pass clots the size of a twenty cent coin, so that she works from home on those days.

Her cycles come every 28 days and last six days, and she has no bleeding between periods and none after intercourse. She has one child and she and her partner plan to start trying for a second pregnancy in about two months, so she does not want anything that prevents conception. Pelvic ultrasound performed last week is reported as a normal uterus with a regular endometrium 6 mm thick, no fibroid and normal ovaries. Cervical screening is up to date and negative. She has no bruising, no family history of bleeding disorder, and no symptoms of thyroid disease.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), ferritin 14 micrograms/L (15-200), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), coagulation screen within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound with a normal uterus, endometrium 6 mm, no fibroid, normal ovaries
data_table.Plans: Intends to conceive in approximately two months

lead_in: Which treatment should you recommend first?

options.text: A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device inserted at the next available appointment
options.rationale: This device is the most effective medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding in a woman with a normal cavity and is first line when contraception is also wanted. It is the wrong choice for someone planning pregnancy within two months, since it would have to be removed almost immediately. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to suppress menstruation entirely
options.rationale: Continuous combined hormonal therapy reliably reduces bleeding but works by preventing ovulation, which directly conflicts with her plan to conceive. It would be a strong option if her priority were contraception rather than fertility. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding

options.text: Endometrial ablation performed as a day case once she has completed her family
options.rationale: Ablation destroys the endometrium and is offered only to women who have definitely completed childbearing, with reliable contraception afterwards because any subsequent pregnancy carries high risk. Her stated plan to conceive rules it out. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding

options.text: Tranexamic acid taken during menstruation, with oral iron to replete her stores
options.rationale: A non-hormonal antifibrinolytic taken only on bleeding days reduces menstrual blood loss substantially and does not interfere with ovulation or conception, which is the constraint that governs this decision. Adding oral iron addresses the low ferritin that is already present despite a haemoglobin near the lower limit. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding

options.text: Referral for hysteroscopy and endometrial sampling before any medical therapy is started
options.rationale: Sampling is indicated for intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, for women over 45, for failed treatment, or when imaging shows a thickened or irregular endometrium, and none of those apply to a regular cycle with a 6 mm endometrium. Investigating first would delay effective treatment without changing it. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding with regular ovulatory cycles, a normal pelvic ultrasound and no intermenstrual bleeding does not require endometrial sampling in a woman under 45. The treatment decision hinges on her reproductive plans: the hormonal intrauterine device and combined hormonal contraception are the most effective options but both are contraceptive, so neither suits a woman intending to conceive within months. Tranexamic acid is taken only on bleeding days, reduces loss by roughly a third to a half, and has no effect on ovulation or on a subsequent pregnancy. Iron repletion is an essential parallel step, since ferritin below 15 micrograms per litre indicates depleted stores even when the haemoglobin is near normal.
key_points: Regular ovulatory bleeding with a normal ultrasound needs no sampling under age 45 without other risk factors
Reproductive intention determines which effective treatments are actually available
Tranexamic acid is taken on bleeding days only and does not impair conception
Treat depleted iron stores in parallel, using ferritin rather than haemoglobin as the trigger
explanation.pearls: Ask when she next wants to conceive before choosing a treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding: if the answer is within a few months, the hormonal intrauterine device and the combined pill both come off the table, leaving tranexamic acid on bleeding days plus iron repletion for a ferritin under 15 micrograms per litre.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding
Therapeutic Guidelines: Gynaecology, Abnormal uterine bleeding

subtopic_detail: maternal seroconversion to a herpesvirus in the first trimester detected on stored booking serum
stem:
You are the registrar in a maternal foetal medicine clinic. A 29-year-old woman at 15 weeks in her second pregnancy is referred after a febrile illness with sore throat and fatigue at 12 weeks that was attributed to a viral infection. Her first child attends childcare.

Serology taken at that time showed immunoglobulin M positive with low avidity immunoglobulin G, while her stored booking serum from 8 weeks was negative for immunoglobulin G, confirming seroconversion during pregnancy. Heterophile antibody and toxoplasma serology are negative. She has no rash and no lymphadenopathy now, and her liver function tests have returned to normal. A detailed ultrasound today shows a structurally normal foetus with normal biometry, normal brain anatomy, no echogenic bowel, no ventriculomegaly and normal amniotic fluid. She is anxious and wants to know what happens next.

data_table.Serology: Immunoglobulin M positive with low avidity immunoglobulin G at 12 weeks, booking serum at 8 weeks immunoglobulin G negative, heterophile and toxoplasma serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound at 15 weeks structurally normal with normal biometry, no ventriculomegaly, no echogenic bowel, normal amniotic fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Repeat maternal serology in four weeks to confirm the seroconversion before acting further
options.rationale: Seroconversion is already proven by a negative immunoglobulin G at 8 weeks followed by a positive result with low avidity, which is exactly the paired evidence that repeat testing would seek. Repeating it wastes four weeks of a pregnancy with a time-critical decision pathway. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy

options.text: Plan amniocentesis for viral nucleic acid testing after 21 weeks and at least six weeks post infection
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid testing is the reference method for establishing whether transmission has occurred, but the virus only becomes reliably detectable once foetal kidneys excrete it into the fluid, so sampling before 21 weeks or too soon after maternal infection gives false negatives. Both conditions are satisfied by scheduling after 21 weeks and at least six weeks from the illness. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy

options.text: Reassure her that the normal scan excludes foetal infection and return to routine care
options.rationale: A normal ultrasound at 15 weeks is reassuring but far from conclusive, because the abnormalities associated with this infection, including ventriculomegaly, intracranial calcification, echogenic bowel and growth restriction, appear weeks to months after transmission. Discharging her now would miss findings that typically emerge in the second half of pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy

options.text: Start maternal valaciclovir and arrange follow up ultrasound examinations every four weeks
options.rationale: High dose valaciclovir is used in some centres to reduce vertical transmission after confirmed first trimester maternal infection and serial ultrasound is part of follow up, so this option contains real elements of care. It nonetheless leaves the central question of whether the foetus is actually infected unanswered, which is what determines counselling and neonatal planning. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy

options.text: Offer chorionic villus sampling this week so that a result is available before 20 weeks
options.rationale: Chorionic villus sampling examines placental tissue and neither reliably diagnoses foetal infection nor is validated for this indication, and placental infection does not equate to foetal infection. It also carries a procedure related loss risk without answering the question. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal diagnostic testing

explanation.summary: Primary cytomegalovirus infection in pregnancy is most often caught from a toddler in childcare and is confirmed by seroconversion between a stored booking sample and a later one, or by immunoglobulin M with low avidity immunoglobulin G. The risk of vertical transmission after primary infection in the first trimester is roughly a third, and of those infected a minority have symptoms at birth, so establishing whether transmission actually occurred changes counselling substantially. Amniocentesis for viral nucleic acid is the diagnostic test, timed after 21 weeks and at least six weeks after maternal infection so that foetal renal excretion makes the virus detectable. A normal early ultrasound does not exclude infection, because the characteristic findings appear later, and serial imaging continues regardless of the amniocentesis result.
key_points: Seroconversion between a stored booking serum and a later sample is diagnostic of primary maternal infection
Amniocentesis must be after 21 weeks and at least six weeks after maternal infection to avoid false negatives
A normal second trimester ultrasound does not exclude foetal infection
Placental sampling does not answer whether the foetus is infected
explanation.pearls: Two clocks govern amniocentesis for suspected congenital cytomegalovirus: gestation must be past 21 weeks, and at least six weeks must have elapsed since the maternal illness. Sampling before either clock has run produces a false negative and the false reassurance that follows it.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy

Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Congenital infections

subtopic_detail: monthly abdominal pain with urinary retention in an adolescent who has never menstruated despite full breast development
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department. A 14-year-old girl presents unable to pass urine for 10 hours, with lower abdominal pain. A bladder scan shows 780 mL of retained urine and a catheter has drained it with immediate relief.

She has never had a period. Her mother says her breasts started developing about three years ago and she has had pubic and axillary hair for two years. For the past six months she has had cramping lower abdominal pain lasting three to four days, arriving at roughly monthly intervals and worsening each time. On abdominal examination there is a smooth suprapubic mass palpable 4 cm above the pubic symphysis, which remains after the bladder has been emptied. She is otherwise well, her height is on the 60th centile, and she has no galactorrhoea, no hirsutism, no headaches and no visual symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Breast and pubic hair development complete for age, smooth suprapubic mass persisting after bladder drainage, no hirsutism
data_table.History: Primary amenorrhoea with six months of cyclical monthly pain, 10 hours of urinary retention relieved by catheterisation
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, urinalysis with no nitrites or leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure follicle stimulating hormone and prolactin and arrange endocrine outpatient review
options.rationale: Hormonal investigation is the right pathway for primary amenorrhoea with absent or delayed secondary sexual characteristics, which would point to gonadal or pituitary failure. Her development is complete and she is having cyclical pain, so the ovaries are clearly functioning and the problem is mechanical. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress the cyclical pain and review in three months
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression would reduce the pain by stopping endometrial shedding, but the accumulated blood behind an obstruction remains and continues to distend the tract. Masking the symptom of an obstructed outflow allows retrograde flow and endometriosis to progress. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea

options.text: Inspect the introitus and arrange pelvic ultrasound to define the level of the obstruction
options.rationale: Cyclical pain with primary amenorrhoea, complete secondary sexual development and a persisting suprapubic mass indicates an obstructed genital tract with blood accumulating behind it, and gentle external inspection plus ultrasound identifies whether the obstruction is a bulging imperforate hymen, a transverse vaginal septum or a more complex anomaly. That distinction determines whether simple hymenotomy suffices or whether formal surgery with magnetic resonance imaging and specialist input is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea

options.text: Request a karyotype for suspected complete androgen insensitivity presenting as amenorrhoea
options.rationale: Complete androgen insensitivity produces breast development with sparse or absent pubic and axillary hair, and there is no uterus, so cyclical pain and a haematometra cannot occur. Her normal sexual hair and cyclical pain both argue against it. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea

options.text: Arrange an indwelling catheter for a week and repeat the trial of void in the outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Repeated catheterisation manages the consequence while the cause continues to enlarge, and the retention will recur as soon as the next accumulation occurs. Definitive relief comes from draining the obstructed tract, not the bladder. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics and cyclical pelvic pain points to obstruction of the genital outflow tract, in which menstrual blood accumulates in the vagina and uterus and eventually presses on the bladder neck to cause retention. The commonest cause is an imperforate hymen, which appears as a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus and is treated by hymenotomy, but a transverse vaginal septum or more complex Mullerian anomaly needs formal surgical planning and often magnetic resonance imaging and renal tract assessment because associated urinary anomalies are common. External inspection plus pelvic ultrasound establishes the level and extent of the obstruction, and definitive drainage is arranged without delay, since prolonged obstruction promotes retrograde menstruation and endometriosis. Endocrine investigation belongs to the separate pathway of amenorrhoea with absent or delayed secondary sexual development.
key_points: Complete secondary sexual development with cyclical pain means the ovaries work and the outflow is blocked
Urinary retention in an adolescent girl should prompt examination of the introitus
Ultrasound with inspection determines whether hymenotomy will suffice or formal surgery is needed
Associated renal tract anomalies are common with more proximal Mullerian obstructions
explanation.pearls: An adolescent girl in urinary retention with a suprapubic mass that persists after catheterisation needs her introitus inspected before any blood test: a bulging bluish membrane is an imperforate hymen relieved by hymenotomy, while a normal introitus with a distended upper vagina means a septum and formal surgical planning.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea
RCH CPG: Gynaecological conditions in adolescence

subtopic_detail: choice of contraception before discharge on day two for a fully breastfeeding woman with a raised body mass index
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward. A 33-year-old woman is due for discharge on day two after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her third child. She is fully breastfeeding and tells you she does not want another pregnancy soon and would prefer to leave hospital with contraception organised.

Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and she had gestational diabetes managed with metformin, which has been stopped. She smoked until she found out she was pregnant and has not resumed. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no migraine, and her blood pressure has been normal throughout. She says that with two toddlers at home she is certain she will forget daily tablets, and that she has never used a device before and does not want anything inserted into the uterus today.

data_table.History: Day two postpartum, fully breastfeeding, gestational diabetes on metformin now ceased, ex-smoker
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, uterus well contracted, lochia normal
data_table.Preferences: Wants contraception before discharge, expects poor tablet adherence, declines intrauterine insertion today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraception to provide before discharge?

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill started today with the first dose given on the ward
options.rationale: Oestrogen containing contraception is avoided in the first three weeks postpartum because venous thromboembolism risk is highest then, and her body mass index adds to that risk. It is also a daily tablet, which is the one thing she has told you will fail. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Reliance on full breastfeeding with amenorrhoea as contraception for the first six months
options.rationale: Lactational amenorrhoea is genuinely effective but only while all three conditions hold together: full breastfeeding, continuing amenorrhoea, and under six months postpartum, and it fails as soon as any one lapses. Offering it as the plan for a woman who wants certainty leaves her exposed the moment feeding patterns change. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: A progestogen-only pill dispensed on discharge with the first tablet taken on day 21
options.rationale: This is a safe option in breastfeeding and is often used, but it is once again a daily tablet in a woman who has told you she will forget, and it leaves a gap between discharge and starting. Adherence, not safety, is what rules it out here. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: An etonogestrel implant inserted in the ward before she goes home today
options.rationale: A progestogen-only implant can be inserted at any time postpartum including immediately after birth, does not affect milk supply or infant growth, and removes the adherence problem she has identified. It also suits a woman whose body mass index and recent pregnancy make oestrogen containing methods less attractive in the early weeks. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Condoms until the six week check, when longer acting options can be discussed properly
options.rationale: Barrier methods are a reasonable interim measure but are user dependent and many women do not return for the six week visit, which is precisely when unplanned pregnancies occur. She is asking for a method now and there is an effective one available before discharge. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance

explanation.summary: Postpartum contraception is best provided before the woman leaves hospital, since ovulation can resume from around day 21 in women who are not fully breastfeeding and attendance at later visits is unreliable. Progestogen-only methods, including the implant, are category one in breastfeeding at any time postpartum and do not reduce milk supply. Combined hormonal methods are avoided in the first three weeks because of venous thromboembolism risk, with the caution extended to six weeks when additional risk factors such as obesity, caesarean birth or smoking are present. Lactational amenorrhoea requires full breastfeeding, continuing amenorrhoea and a postpartum interval under six months, and ceases to be reliable once any of these lapses.
key_points: Progestogen-only implants can be inserted immediately postpartum without affecting lactation
Avoid oestrogen containing contraception for at least three weeks postpartum, longer with added risk factors
Lactational amenorrhoea only works while all three of its conditions hold simultaneously
Provide the method before discharge rather than deferring to a visit that may not happen
explanation.pearls: Treat the postnatal ward as the contraception appointment: an etonogestrel implant can go in before discharge, is safe from day one of breastfeeding, and sidesteps both the three week oestrogen window and the daily adherence problem that defeats the progestogen-only pill in a household with toddlers.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidance
RANZCOG: Postpartum contraception

subtopic_detail: threads no longer felt after an intrauterine device insertion with a negative pregnancy test and no expulsion witnessed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman who had a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device inserted eight months ago. She could feel the threads at first but has not been able to find them for the past two months, and you cannot see them at the cervical os on speculum examination.

Insertion was described in the notes as more difficult than usual, with the sound passing to 9 cm and the patient reporting sharp pain at that point. Her periods have been very light throughout and she has no pelvic pain, no fever, no abnormal discharge and no dyspareunia. She has never seen the device pass and has not noticed it in the toilet or on a pad. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. She has been sexually active without other contraception, and she would like to keep using this method if it is still in place.

data_table.Examination: No threads visible at the cervical os, uterus non-tender, no adnexal mass, no cervical excitation
data_table.History: Difficult insertion eight months ago with sharp pain as the sound passed to 9 cm, threads felt initially then lost
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What should you do next?

options.text: Reassure her that the threads have simply retracted and review at her next cervical screening test
options.rationale: Threads retracting into the canal is the commonest explanation and is often the outcome, but that conclusion can only be reached once the device has been shown to be inside the uterus. Assuming it without imaging leaves her unprotected if it has been expelled or has perforated. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Attempt blind removal with thread retrieval forceps and insert a new device at the same visit
options.rationale: Instrumenting the cavity before the device has been localised risks damaging a partially embedded device or attempting retrieval of one that is not there. Retrieval procedures follow imaging, not the other way round. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Arrange pelvic ultrasound, advise additional contraception, and image the abdomen if it is not seen
options.rationale: Missing threads means the device is retracted, expelled or has perforated, and ultrasound distinguishes the first from the others while additional contraception covers the interval because expulsion cannot be excluded until then. If ultrasound does not show the device in the uterus, a plain abdominal radiograph is required, since a perforated device lies somewhere in the abdomen and this history of a difficult insertion with sharp pain raises that possibility. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Refer directly for laparoscopy on the basis of the difficult insertion and the lost threads
options.rationale: Laparoscopic retrieval is the treatment for a device confirmed to lie in the peritoneal cavity, and proceeding to surgery before imaging would operate on many women whose device is simply sitting normally with retracted threads. Imaging has to come first. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance

options.text: Take endocervical swabs and treat empirically for pelvic infection before any imaging is arranged
options.rationale: Infection would present with pain, fever, discharge or cervical excitation, and she has none of these. Empirical antibiotics neither locate the device nor restore contraceptive cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pelvic inflammatory disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pelvic inflammatory disease

explanation.summary: Non-visible threads after intrauterine device insertion have three explanations: the threads have retracted into the canal or cavity with the device correctly sited, the device has been expelled, or it has perforated the uterus and lies in the abdomen. Pregnancy must be excluded first, and additional contraception is advised until the device is confirmed to be in place. Pelvic ultrasound is the initial investigation, and if the device is not seen within the uterus a plain abdominal radiograph is mandatory, because the device is radio-opaque and an expelled device must be distinguished from a perforated one. Perforation is uncommon but is more likely after a difficult insertion, when breastfeeding, and in the early postpartum period, and a device confirmed in the peritoneal cavity is retrieved laparoscopically.
key_points: Exclude pregnancy and advise additional contraception before investigating missing threads
Ultrasound first; a device not seen in the uterus requires an abdominal radiograph
A radiograph distinguishes expulsion from perforation, since the device is radio-opaque
Difficult insertion, breastfeeding and recent birth increase the risk of perforation
explanation.pearls: Missing intrauterine device threads are not resolved by ultrasound alone: if the device is not visible in the uterus, an abdominal radiograph is compulsory, because the only other explanations are expulsion and perforation and you cannot tell them apart without seeing whether the device is still in the abdomen.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception clinical guidance
RANZCOG: Long acting reversible contraception
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pelvic inflammatory disease

subtopic_detail: perineal trauma extending into the external anal sphincter identified immediately after an assisted birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 27-year-old woman has just had a forceps birth of a 4100 g baby in the occipitoposterior position after a prolonged second stage, under an epidural that is still working well.

You perform a systematic perineal and rectal examination immediately after birth. There is a midline tear extending through the perineal body, and on rectal examination you can feel a defect involving about half the thickness of the external anal sphincter, with the internal sphincter and the rectal mucosa intact. Bleeding is moderate and the uterus is well contracted after active management of the third stage. The woman is comfortable, her observations are normal, and the baby is on her chest feeding. The midwife asks whether you will repair the tear in the room.

data_table.Examination: Midline perineal tear through the perineal body with a partial thickness defect of the external anal sphincter, internal sphincter and rectal mucosa intact
data_table.Birth details: Forceps birth, occipitoposterior position, birth weight 4100 g, prolonged second stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this perineal injury?

options.text: Repair in theatre with regional anaesthesia, a single dose of intravenous antibiotic and laxatives after
options.rationale: Injury involving the anal sphincter is repaired in an operating theatre with adequate regional or general anaesthesia, good lighting, assistance and appropriate instruments, because relaxation and exposure determine whether the sphincter ends are apposed correctly. Prophylactic intravenous antibiotic at repair and a postoperative laxative regimen both reduce wound breakdown and later incontinence. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair in the birth room using the working epidural, with oral antibiotics started afterwards
options.rationale: A functioning epidural provides analgesia but not the muscle relaxation and exposure needed to retrieve retracted sphincter ends, and birth room lighting and instruments are usually inadequate. Repair performed under these conditions is associated with worse continence outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair only the perineal body now and refer for delayed sphincter repair at six weeks postpartum
options.rationale: Delayed or secondary repair is the salvage route for injuries recognised late or for failed primary repair, and it has poorer functional results than repair at the time of birth. Recognising the injury now is precisely the opportunity that should not be deferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Leave the tear to heal by secondary intention with pelvic floor physiotherapy from day two
options.rationale: Conservative management is appropriate for superficial labial or first degree tears that are haemostatic and well apposed, not for a disrupted sphincter. Physiotherapy supports recovery after repair but cannot restore a divided muscle ring. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Arrange endoanal ultrasound before repair to define the extent of the sphincter disruption
options.rationale: Endoanal ultrasound is valuable for assessing residual defects and symptoms after repair, or before a subsequent birth, but it is not required when the defect has been felt directly at the time of injury. Waiting for imaging would delay a repair that should happen without unnecessary delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: Every woman should have a systematic perineal and rectal examination after vaginal birth, because unrecognised anal sphincter injury is the main preventable cause of later faecal incontinence. A partial thickness external sphincter defect is classified as a third degree tear and is repaired in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia, where relaxation, lighting and assistance allow the retracted muscle ends to be identified and apposed. A single dose of intravenous broad spectrum antibiotic at the time of repair, followed by laxatives and physiotherapy, reduces wound breakdown and improves functional outcome. Forceps birth, occipitoposterior position, a large baby and a prolonged second stage are the classic risk factors that should raise suspicion before the examination is even performed.
key_points: Perform a rectal examination after every vaginal birth to avoid missing sphincter injury
Sphincter repair belongs in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia, not in the birth room
Give a single intravenous antibiotic dose at repair and prescribe laxatives afterwards
Delayed repair produces worse continence outcomes than repair at the time of injury
explanation.pearls: A working epidural is not a reason to repair a sphincter tear in the birth room: the epidural gives analgesia without relaxation, and the retracted external sphincter ends need theatre conditions, a single intravenous antibiotic dose at repair, and a laxative regimen afterwards if the woman is to stay continent.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Surgical prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: bleeding after intercourse with a red ring around the os in a pill user whose screening is current and negative
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 25-year-old woman who has noticed light bleeding after intercourse on about half a dozen occasions in the past four months, described as a smear of blood rather than a flow.

She has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill for three years with no missed pills, and her withdrawal bleeds are regular and light. She has no pelvic pain, no dyspareunia, no abnormal discharge and no intermenstrual bleeding at other times. On speculum examination the cervix has a symmetrical red velvety area extending circumferentially around the external os with a smooth border, and it bleeds slightly when touched with a swab. There is no ulceration, no irregular mass and no friable exophytic lesion. Her human papillomavirus screening test three months ago was negative for oncogenic types, and nucleic acid tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea taken today are both negative.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical circumferential red velvety area around the external os with a smooth border, contact bleeding on swabbing, no ulceration or irregular mass
data_table.Investigations: Human papillomavirus screening negative for oncogenic types three months ago, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid tests negative
data_table.History: Combined oral contraceptive pill for three years, regular light withdrawal bleeds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently for colposcopy and directed biopsy of the abnormal looking cervical area
options.rationale: Colposcopy is required when screening detects oncogenic types, when the cervix looks clinically suspicious with an irregular friable or ulcerated lesion, or when symptoms persist after other causes are excluded. A symmetrical smooth bordered red zone with recent negative screening does not meet those criteria. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: Explain the finding, review in three months, and investigate further if bleeding persists
options.rationale: Columnar epithelium everted onto the outer cervix is a normal variant that is common with oestrogen exposure from the pill and bleeds on contact because the epithelium is a single cell layer thick, so explanation with planned review is sufficient once infection and screening have been cleared. Bleeding that persists beyond that review then justifies colposcopy regardless of the screening result. (Source: RANZCOG: Postcoital bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Postcoital bleeding

options.text: Treat the cervix with cryotherapy or diathermy ablation at this visit to stop the bleeding
options.rationale: Ablation is occasionally offered for troublesome persistent contact bleeding after other causes are excluded, but it is not a first response and causes discharge, and occasionally stenosis, for a finding that is physiological. Starting with treatment skips the observation period that resolves most cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Postcoital bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Postcoital bleeding

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus screening test now given the abnormal cervical appearance
options.rationale: Repeating a screening test three months after a negative result adds nothing, since the interval is far too short for a clinically relevant change and the program interval is five years. A visibly suspicious cervix is assessed by colposcopy rather than by repeating screening. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: Stop the combined oral contraceptive pill and change to a copper intrauterine device instead
options.rationale: Oestrogen exposure does contribute to eversion of the columnar epithelium, but stopping an effective contraceptive she is happy with is a disproportionate response to intermittent light contact bleeding. A copper device also increases menstrual loss, which is unlikely to please her. (Source: RANZCOG: Postcoital bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Postcoital bleeding

explanation.summary: Bleeding after intercourse requires exclusion of cervical cancer, cervical infection and, in older women, endometrial pathology, but in a young woman it is most often caused by ectropion, the physiological eversion of fragile columnar epithelium onto the ectocervix. The appearance is symmetrical and smooth bordered with contact bleeding, and it is common with combined oral contraceptive use and in pregnancy. Once chlamydia and gonorrhoea are excluded and cervical screening is current and negative, explanation with a planned review is appropriate, and persistent symptoms at that review warrant colposcopy even if screening remains negative, since screening detects the virus rather than an established cancer. Ablative treatment is reserved for persistent troublesome bleeding after other causes have been excluded.
key_points: A symmetrical smooth bordered red zone around the os is ectropion, not a suspicious lesion
Exclude chlamydia and gonorrhoea and confirm that screening is current before reassuring
Persistent postcoital bleeding warrants colposcopy even when screening is negative
Ablation is a later option for troublesome bleeding, not a first line treatment
explanation.pearls: A negative human papillomavirus screen does not close the question when postcoital bleeding persists: screening detects viral infection, not an established cancer, so bleeding that continues past a planned three month review earns a colposcopy whatever the screening result said.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Postcoital bleeding
National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

subtopic_detail: screening for diabetes at 26 weeks in a woman who has had sleeve gastrectomy and gets symptoms after sugary drinks
stem:
You are the registrar in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 34-year-old woman at 25 weeks in her first pregnancy attends to arrange her routine screening for diabetes in pregnancy. She had a sleeve gastrectomy three years ago and has maintained a weight loss of 40 kg.

She tells you that sugary drinks make her feel sweaty, shaky, nauseated and lightheaded about 20 minutes later, and that she has passed out once after a milkshake. She takes a pregnancy multivitamin, oral iron, and monthly vitamin B12 injections. Her booking bloods showed a normal full blood count and a glycated haemoglobin of 5.2 per cent. Her blood pressure has been normal and the foetus is growing along the 50th centile on ultrasound. She asks what will happen at her appointment next week and whether she has to drink the glucose solution.

data_table.History: Sleeve gastrectomy three years ago, 40 kg weight loss maintained, symptoms suggestive of dumping after sugary drinks including one syncopal episode
data_table.Investigations: Booking glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent (less than 6.0), full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin, oral iron, monthly vitamin B12 injections

lead_in: How should she be screened for diabetes in this pregnancy?

options.text: Proceed with the standard 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks as for any pregnancy
options.rationale: The standard oral load is poorly tolerated after bariatric surgery because rapid gastric emptying produces early hypoglycaemia and vasomotor symptoms, and the resulting curve is difficult to interpret against thresholds derived from unoperated women. Her syncopal episode after a milkshake predicts exactly this. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

options.text: Repeat the glycated haemoglobin at 26 weeks and treat a result of 5.9 per cent or above
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin falls physiologically in pregnancy and is further distorted by the accelerated red cell turnover of iron therapy, so it lacks the sensitivity needed to detect the degree of hyperglycaemia that matters for the foetus. It is useful at booking to detect pre-existing diabetes, not as the screening test in the second trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

options.text: Use a week of capillary glucose monitoring fasting and after meals instead of a glucose load
options.rationale: Home glucose profiling captures the fasting and postprandial values that drive foetal growth without provoking the rapid transit reaction, which is why it is the accepted alternative after bariatric surgery. A week of paired fasting and post meal readings identifies the women who need dietary and pharmacological treatment and can simply be continued if abnormal. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

options.text: Omit screening entirely because her preoperative obesity has resolved and her booking test was normal
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery reduces but does not abolish the risk of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy, and these women remain at risk of small for gestational age infants and nutritional deficiency needing surveillance. A normal booking glycated haemoglobin excludes pre-existing diabetes but says nothing about the third trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

options.text: Perform a fasting venous glucose alone at 26 weeks and screen no further if it is below 5.1 mmol/L
options.rationale: A single fasting value misses the women whose abnormality is postprandial, and after this operation the postprandial pattern is precisely where the abnormality tends to sit. Relying on it alone would falsely reassure in the group most likely to have late peaks. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

explanation.summary: After sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass, an oral glucose load empties rapidly into the small bowel, producing an early exaggerated peak followed by reactive hypoglycaemia with sweating, palpitations and sometimes syncope. This makes the standard oral glucose tolerance test both unpleasant and uninterpretable, so Australian practice substitutes a week of capillary glucose monitoring with fasting and postprandial readings around the usual screening window. Glycated haemoglobin is used at booking to detect undiagnosed pre-existing diabetes but is insensitive later in pregnancy, particularly alongside iron therapy. These pregnancies also need attention to micronutrient status and to foetal growth, since small for gestational age infants are more common after bariatric surgery.
key_points: Rapid gastric emptying after bariatric surgery makes the standard glucose load unreliable and poorly tolerated
A week of fasting and postprandial capillary readings is the accepted alternative
Glycated haemoglobin is a booking test for pre-existing diabetes, not a second trimester screen
Monitor growth and micronutrients as well as glucose in pregnancies after bariatric surgery
explanation.pearls: Ask any pregnant woman with previous bariatric surgery what happens 20 minutes after a sugary drink: sweating, palpitations and lightheadedness mean the 75 g load will be both intolerable and uninterpretable, and a week of fasting plus two hour postprandial capillary glucose readings replaces it.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus
RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy
Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society: Consensus recommendations

subtopic_detail: suprapubic pain relieved by voiding with repeatedly sterile urine after multiple antibiotic courses
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman referred with two years of bladder symptoms. She passes urine about 14 times during the day and three times at night, and describes constant suprapubic pressure that builds as the bladder fills and eases for a while after she voids.

She has had seven courses of antibiotics in the past year for presumed urinary infection, with temporary improvement she attributes to the accompanying fluid intake. Every midstream sample sent in that time has been reported as no growth, including two taken while she was symptomatic and off antibiotics. She has no haematuria, no weight loss, no fevers and no flank pain, and she has never smoked. A bladder diary shows small voided volumes of 100 to 150 mL with no leakage and no urgency incontinence episodes. Renal tract ultrasound with a post void residual of 20 mL is normal, and urine cytology is negative.

data_table.Symptom pattern: Suprapubic pain worsening with bladder filling and relieved by voiding, frequency 14 times daily and three times nightly
data_table.Investigations: Repeated midstream cultures with no growth including two while symptomatic off antibiotics, urine cytology negative
data_table.Imaging: Renal tract ultrasound normal with post void residual 20 mL, bladder diary showing voided volumes 100 to 150 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe low dose nitrofurantoin nightly for six months as prophylaxis against recurrent infection
options.rationale: Continuous prophylaxis is used for culture proven recurrent infection, and repeated sterile cultures taken while symptomatic exclude that diagnosis here. Six further months of antibiotic would add adverse effects and resistance without touching the mechanism of her pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Recurrent urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Recurrent urinary tract infection

options.text: Start solifenacin and review the response to antimuscarinic therapy in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic treatment targets detrusor overactivity, whose defining symptom is sudden compelling urgency with or without incontinence rather than pain that builds with filling. Her diary records no urgency incontinence, so the drug addresses a symptom she does not have. (Source: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome

options.text: Arrange urgent cystoscopy and computed tomography urography to exclude bladder malignancy
options.rationale: Urothelial malignancy is the diagnosis to exclude when there is visible or persistent non-visible haematuria, especially with smoking history or age above 45, and none of those apply here. Cystoscopy has a place later in assessing this syndrome but as an urgent cancer investigation it is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome

options.text: Begin bladder retraining and dietary trigger avoidance with low dose amitriptyline at night
options.rationale: Pain that builds with bladder filling and eases on voiding, with sterile urine and small voided volumes, is bladder pain syndrome, and first line treatment combines behavioural measures with a neuromodulating agent. Amitriptyline at low dose addresses the visceral pain and improves sleep, while retraining and avoidance of dietary triggers extend voided volumes over weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome

options.text: Refer for intravesical botulinum toxin injection into the detrusor muscle under cystoscopy
options.rationale: Intradetrusor botulinum toxin is a third line treatment for refractory overactive bladder and is considered in this syndrome only after conservative and oral therapies have failed. Offering it now skips the treatments that help most women and carries a risk of retention requiring self catheterisation. (Source: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome

explanation.summary: Bladder pain syndrome is diagnosed clinically from persistent pain perceived to arise from the bladder, worsening with filling and relieved at least temporarily by voiding, together with frequency and repeatedly sterile urine. The defining contrast with overactive bladder is that the driving symptom is pain rather than urgency, which is why antimuscarinic drugs disappoint. Repeated empirical antibiotic courses are the commonest pattern of mismanagement, and cultures taken while symptomatic and off antibiotics are the evidence that settles it. First line treatment combines bladder retraining, avoidance of individual dietary triggers, and low dose amitriptyline, with cystoscopy, intravesical therapies and pain clinic referral reserved for those who do not respond.
key_points: Pain that builds with filling and eases with voiding distinguishes this from overactive bladder
Sterile cultures taken while symptomatic and off antibiotics rule out recurrent infection
First line therapy is behavioural plus low dose amitriptyline, not antimuscarinics
Haematuria, age above 45 or smoking would redirect the workup toward malignancy
explanation.pearls: Two facts settle most chronic bladder symptom referrals: whether the dominant symptom is pain or urgency, and whether any culture has ever grown an organism while the patient was symptomatic and off antibiotics. Pain that eases on voiding with repeatedly sterile urine is bladder pain syndrome, treated with retraining, trigger avoidance and low dose amitriptyline.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Bladder pain syndrome
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Recurrent urinary tract infection

subtopic_detail: recurrent hair pulling with visible patchy loss and mounting tension before pulling in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old girl brought by her mother after the school nurse noticed patchy hair loss. The girl acknowledges, once her mother steps out, that she pulls hair from her scalp while doing homework and watching television.

She describes a build-up of tension before pulling and relief afterwards, followed by shame. She has tried to stop several times and has not managed more than a few days. She does not swallow the hair and has no abdominal pain. On examination there are irregular patches of thinned hair over the right frontoparietal scalp with hairs of varying lengths and no scaling, no scarring, no erythema and no broken hairs elsewhere. She denies low mood, has friends, is doing well academically, and there is no self harm, no restrictive eating and no substance use. Thyroid function and iron studies requested by the nurse are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Irregular patches of thinned scalp hair with hairs of varying length, no scaling, scarring or erythema, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, engaged, no suicidal ideation, no restrictive eating, no substance use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start N-acetylcysteine at a standard adult dose and review the pulling in twelve weeks
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine has shown benefit for hair pulling in some adult trials and is sometimes used as an adjunct, but the adolescent evidence is weak and it has not displaced behavioural therapy as first line. Offering a supplement first also implies that the behaviour cannot be modified directly, which is the opposite of the message that helps. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Begin self monitoring of pulling episodes and refer for habit reversal training now
options.rationale: Habit reversal training, in which awareness training, a competing physical response and stimulus control are taught together, is the first line treatment for hair pulling disorder at every age and outperforms medication. Starting a record of when and where pulling happens gives the therapist the pattern to work with and begins the awareness training component immediately. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review the response after six weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder itself but have not shown consistent benefit for hair pulling, which is a body focused repetitive behaviour rather than a compulsion driven by an obsession. Medication is considered when behavioural therapy has failed or when a comorbid disorder such as depression is present, and she has neither. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Prescribe topical minoxidil solution to the affected scalp and review the regrowth in three months
options.rationale: Topical minoxidil treats androgenetic hair loss, which produces diffuse thinning rather than irregular patches with hairs of different lengths. Regrowth here depends on stopping the pulling, and prescribing a topical agent implies that the scalp rather than the behaviour is the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders

options.text: Arrange a scalp biopsy to distinguish scarring from non-scarring causes of the hair loss
options.rationale: Biopsy is useful when the cause of patchy alopecia is uncertain, particularly to identify scarring processes, but here the girl has described the mechanism directly and the scalp shows no scarring or inflammation. Investigating further risks conveying disbelief at the moment she has disclosed something difficult. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders

explanation.summary: Hair pulling disorder is classified among the obsessive compulsive and related disorders and is characterised by recurrent pulling with repeated attempts to stop, often preceded by tension and followed by relief. The examination findings of irregular patches containing hairs of varying lengths, with a normal non-scarred scalp, distinguish it from alopecia areata and from fungal infection. First line treatment is habit reversal training, a behavioural package of awareness training, a competing response and stimulus control, which outperforms medication in this condition. Asking specifically about swallowing hair matters because trichobezoar can cause obstruction, and screening for depression and anxiety is routine since comorbidity is common.
key_points: Hairs of varying length in irregular patches with a normal scalp point to pulling rather than alopecia areata
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms serotonin reuptake inhibitors
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are reserved for comorbid disorders or failed behavioural therapy
Ask about swallowing hair, since trichobezoar can cause gastrointestinal obstruction
explanation.pearls: Ask two questions when you see patchy hair loss with intact scalp skin: does the tension build before and ease after, and does she swallow the hair? A yes to the first makes habit reversal training the treatment, and a yes to the second makes an abdominal examination for a trichobezoar urgent.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders

subtopic_detail: deliberate under-dosing of insulin for weight control with recurrent ketoacidosis and normal body weight
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to see a 19-year-old woman on the medical ward, admitted with her fourth episode of diabetic ketoacidosis in eight months. She has had type 1 diabetes since she was nine.

Her glycated haemoglobin has risen from 7.4 to 11.8 per cent over two years. On interview she tells you that she reduces or skips her long acting insulin because she gains weight whenever her glucose is well controlled, and she describes checking her stomach and thighs in the mirror many times a day and feeling disgusted. She denies vomiting, laxative use and binge eating. Her body mass index is 21.5 kg/m2 and her weight has been stable. She is low in mood and tearful but denies suicidal ideation, and she has been avoiding her diabetes clinic appointments because she expects to be told off about her numbers.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 11.8 per cent (less than 7.0 target), venous bicarbonate now 24 mmol/L (22-32), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21.5 kg/m2, weight stable, no parotid swelling, no dental erosion, no Russell sign
data_table.Mental state: Low mood, tearful, body checking many times daily, no suicidal ideation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Refer for joint eating disorder and diabetes care with a shared plan for insulin restarting
options.rationale: Insulin restriction for weight control is an eating disorder expressed through diabetes, so treatment has to be delivered jointly by a service able to address body image and by the diabetes team able to reintroduce insulin at a pace that limits the fluid shift, oedema and neuropathic pain that rapid normalisation causes. Addressing either side alone reproduces the pattern of escalating glycated haemoglobin and repeated admissions. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Increase her long acting insulin dose and arrange weekly endocrinology review by telephone
options.rationale: Adjusting the prescription treats the number rather than the reason the insulin is not being taken, and prescribing more of a drug she is deliberately omitting predictably fails. Dose optimisation becomes useful once the eating disorder is being treated alongside it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Start sertraline for depression and review her mood in four weeks in the outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Depressive symptoms are common alongside this presentation and may need treatment, but an antidepressant alone does not alter insulin restriction, which is the behaviour causing life threatening episodes. Mood treatment sits within the joint plan rather than replacing it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Apply mental health legislation for involuntary treatment because of the risk to her life
options.rationale: Compulsory treatment is reserved for patients who lack capacity or pose an imminent risk that cannot be managed voluntarily, and she is engaging, disclosing and willing to talk. Beginning with legislation would damage the therapeutic relationship that her long term recovery depends on. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Discharge with diabetes educator follow up and a written plan for sick day management
options.rationale: Sick day education addresses ketoacidosis triggered by intercurrent illness, whereas hers is triggered by deliberate omission, so the plan targets the wrong mechanism. Education alone has already failed across three previous admissions. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

explanation.summary: Deliberate insulin restriction for weight control is a disordered eating behaviour unique to type 1 diabetes and is easily missed because body weight is normal and the classic purging signs are absent. The clues are a rising glycated haemoglobin, repeated admissions with ketoacidosis, clinic non-attendance, and body checking with weight-related reasoning about insulin. It carries a substantially increased risk of retinopathy, nephropathy and early death, which makes it more dangerous than the numbers alone suggest. Effective management is joint: an eating disorder service for the body image and behavioural work, and the diabetes team to restart insulin gradually, since rapid normalisation of glucose can cause oedema, worsening retinopathy and neuropathic pain that reinforces avoidance.
key_points: Normal body weight does not exclude an eating disorder in type 1 diabetes
Rising glycated haemoglobin with repeated ketoacidosis and clinic avoidance is the pattern to recognise
Ask directly about omitting insulin to control weight, since it is rarely volunteered
Reintroduce insulin gradually within a joint eating disorder and diabetes plan
explanation.pearls: Ask every young person with type 1 diabetes and recurrent ketoacidosis whether they ever take less insulin than prescribed to influence their weight. A yes reframes the admission from poor adherence to an eating disorder, and the treatment becomes joint eating disorder and diabetes care with deliberately gradual insulin reintroduction.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders
InsideOut Institute: Eating disorders and diabetes
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Type 1 diabetes

subtopic_detail: request to assess whether a man with early dementia can validly instruct a solicitor to change his will
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a memory clinic. A solicitor writes asking whether a 79-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease, diagnosed 14 months ago, has the capacity to change his will. He wants to leave a larger share to the daughter who has been caring for him and less to his two other children.

His Mini-Mental State Examination score was 23 out of 30 six months ago. In the consultation he knows he is making a will and what a will does, names all three children and his approximate assets including the house and a superannuation balance, and explains that the caring daughter has driven him to appointments for three years while the others live interstate. He acknowledges the others may be upset. There is no delusional content, no persecutory belief about the other children, and no evidence that anyone has pressured him, and he attends alone. His mood is euthymic and he is not acutely unwell.

data_table.Cognition: Mini-Mental State Examination 23 out of 30 six months ago, mild Alzheimer disease diagnosed 14 months ago
data_table.Interview findings: Understands the nature of a will, identifies all three children and approximate assets, gives a coherent reason for the change, anticipates the reaction of the others
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no delusions, no evidence of coercion, attends the appointment alone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the solicitor?

options.text: Advise that the diagnosis of dementia in itself removes his ability to make a valid will
options.rationale: Capacity is decision specific and is not abolished by a diagnosis, and many people with mild dementia retain the ability to make a will. Treating the diagnosis as decisive would deny him a legal right he still holds. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

options.text: Report that he demonstrates the specific abilities required, documenting the reasoning in detail
options.rationale: The test is whether he understands the nature of the act, appreciates the extent of his property, recalls those who might expect to benefit, and is free of a disorder of mind that distorts the disposal, all of which he demonstrates in this interview. Recording his own words against each element is what makes the opinion useful if the will is later contested. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

options.text: Recommend that his caring daughter be appointed to make the decision on his behalf
options.rationale: A substitute decision maker can never make a will on another person's behalf, and appointing the principal beneficiary to any decision making role here would create a clear conflict of interest. Substitute decision making applies to health, accommodation and financial decisions, not testamentary ones. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

options.text: Suggest repeat cognitive testing and defer any opinion until the score has been rechecked
options.rationale: Screening scores describe cognitive performance but do not determine capacity for a specific decision, and no cut-off on a brief test establishes or excludes testamentary capacity. Deferring for a number risks him losing the ability to make the will while waiting. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

options.text: Decline to comment because deciding testamentary capacity is a matter for the courts alone
options.rationale: A court makes the final legal determination, usually long after the person has died, but it does so largely on the strength of contemporaneous clinical assessment. Declining to assess removes the very evidence that protects his wishes from later challenge. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

explanation.summary: Testamentary capacity is assessed against four established elements: understanding the nature and effect of making a will, knowing the extent of the property being disposed of, comprehending and appreciating the claims of those who might expect to benefit, and being free from any disorder of mind that perverts the disposal. It is decision specific and time specific, so neither a dementia diagnosis nor a screening score determines it. A man who explains his assets, names all potential beneficiaries, gives a coherent and non-delusional reason for favouring one, and anticipates the reaction of the others satisfies the test despite mild impairment. The clinician's task is to document the reasoning verbatim against each element and to comment on voluntariness, since undue influence is a separate ground for challenge.
key_points: Capacity is decision specific and is not abolished by a diagnosis or a screening score
The four elements concern the nature of the act, the property, the potential claimants and freedom from distorting disorder
A substitute decision maker cannot make a will for another person
Contemporaneous documentation in the person's own words is what withstands later challenge
explanation.pearls: Document the person's own words against each of the four testamentary elements rather than recording a cognitive score: a Mini-Mental State Examination result neither confers nor removes capacity, and it is the verbatim account of assets, beneficiaries and reasons that a court relies on years later.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent
Australian Law Reform Commission: Equality, capacity and disability

subtopic_detail: intense dread of giving birth in a first pregnancy with avoidance of antenatal care and no prior birth trauma
stem:
You are the psychiatrist in a perinatal clinic. A 28-year-old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy is referred by her midwife because she has missed three appointments and becomes distressed whenever labour is mentioned.

She describes intrusive images of dying in childbirth, nightmares about being torn, and panic with palpitations and sweating when she passes the birth suite. She has been avoiding antenatal classes and the hospital tour, and says she has considered not attending for the birth at all. She wanted this pregnancy and is looking forward to the baby. She has no history of sexual assault, no previous birth, no previous trauma and no history of depression or an anxiety disorder, and she is not misusing substances. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 11 with a zero response on the self harm item, and she sleeps poorly only on nights when she has been thinking about labour.

data_table.Symptoms: Intrusive images of dying in childbirth, nightmares, panic on approaching the birth suite, avoidance of classes and appointments
data_table.Screening: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 11 with zero on the self harm item
data_table.History: First pregnancy, no prior trauma or assault, no previous psychiatric history, wanted pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe diazepam to be taken before antenatal visits and again during early labour
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines relieve anticipatory anxiety briefly but reinforce avoidance, and regular use late in pregnancy risks neonatal sedation and withdrawal. Using them as the plan would prevent the graded exposure that actually reduces the fear. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline

options.text: Advise that she request a planned caesarean section so that labour can be avoided altogether
options.rationale: Mode of birth is a decision for the woman with her obstetric team and caesarean birth is a legitimate outcome of that discussion, but recommending it now as the treatment for her fear removes the opportunity to reduce it. Women whose fear is addressed psychologically often choose vaginal birth and report better experiences either way. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean section on maternal request)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Caesarean section on maternal request

options.text: Offer structured psychological therapy for childbirth fear with a birth planning session
options.rationale: Severe fear of childbirth responds to a brief structured psychological intervention that combines cognitive work on catastrophic beliefs with graded exposure to the hospital environment, delivered alongside a midwife-led session that produces a written birth plan. This addresses the avoidance that is currently putting her antenatal care at risk while leaving her choice about mode of birth open. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline

options.text: Start sertraline given the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score and review in six weeks
options.rationale: A score of 11 is below the usual threshold prompting further assessment and her elevated items reflect anxiety about a specific situation rather than pervasive depression, with preserved interest in the pregnancy and the baby. An antidepressant may become appropriate if a depressive or generalised anxiety disorder emerges, but it is not the first response to a focal phobia. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline)
