source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline

options.text: Reassure her that anxiety about a first birth is normal and arrange midwife review at 34 weeks
options.rationale: Ordinary apprehension does not cause someone to miss three appointments, avoid all preparation and consider not presenting for the birth, so normalising it misses a disorder that is already affecting care. Waiting until 34 weeks leaves little time for a therapy that needs several sessions. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Severe fear of childbirth is distinguished from ordinary apprehension by avoidance that damages care: missed appointments, refusal of preparation, and contemplation of not attending for the birth. It occurs both in women with no obstetric history and in those with previous traumatic birth, and it predicts requests for caesarean birth, longer labour and postnatal traumatic stress symptoms. Treatment is psychological and relatively brief, combining cognitive work on catastrophic beliefs with graded exposure, and is most effective when paired with a midwifery session that produces a concrete written birth plan including pain relief preferences and a plan for regaining control. Mode of birth remains the woman's decision and is discussed after the fear has been treated, not instead of treating it.
key_points: Avoidance that disrupts antenatal care separates a phobic disorder from normal apprehension
Brief cognitive and exposure based therapy is first line, ideally started well before term
Pair psychological treatment with a midwife-led session that produces a written birth plan
Antidepressants and benzodiazepines are not the primary treatment for a focal childbirth phobia
explanation.pearls: Missed antenatal appointments are the sign that turns fear of childbirth into a treatable disorder rather than normal nerves. Refer for brief cognitive and exposure based therapy by the mid second trimester and pair it with a midwifery birth planning session, so there is time for several sessions before term.

sources.label: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline
RANZCOG: Caesarean section on maternal request
COPE: Australian perinatal mental health guideline

subtopic_detail: vivid formed visual hallucinations with full insight in an older adult with advanced macular degeneration
stem:
You are the doctor at a residential aged care facility. Staff ask you to review an 84-year-old woman who has been describing children in period costume standing at the end of her bed and patterned brickwork spreading across the wall.

She tells you calmly that she knows they are not really there, that they appear most in the late afternoon and last several minutes, and that she finds them curious rather than frightening. She has advanced age related macular degeneration with vision of 6/60 in both eyes after a recent further decline. She hears nothing unusual, has no delusions and no persecutory ideas, and she is oriented to place and person and gives a clear account of her day. There is no fluctuating attention, no tremor, no rigidity, no falls, no recent change in medication and no urinary symptoms, and her observations and screening bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: No tremor or rigidity, no postural instability, attention sustained through the interview, oriented to place and person
data_table.Vision: Visual acuity 6/60 bilaterally with advanced age related macular degeneration and recent further decline
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, calcium, thyroid function and urinalysis all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start risperidone 0.25 mg at night and review the frequency of the hallucinations in two weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not reliably abolish these hallucinations and expose an older woman to falls, stroke and increased mortality for a symptom she is not distressed by. Their use would also be difficult to justify given she retains full insight. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the brain to exclude an occipital infarct or tumour
options.rationale: Structural imaging is indicated when hallucinations accompany focal neurological signs, headache, seizures or an abrupt change in conscious state, and none are present. Scanning an older person with a classical syndrome yields incidental findings more often than answers. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Treat for delirium with a septic screen, medication review and regular orientation by staff
options.rationale: Delirium is the correct first thought for new hallucinations in an older person, but it requires disturbed attention and a fluctuating course, and her attention is sustained and her account coherent. The negative screening investigations and absence of new medications complete the case against it. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Explain the visual origin of the images, review her vision, and monitor with staff education
options.rationale: Formed visual hallucinations with retained insight and no other psychotic or cognitive features in someone with severe visual loss are generated by the deafferented visual cortex, and explanation itself is the main treatment because the distress comes mostly from fearing madness. Optimising remaining vision, improving lighting and environmental stimulation, and teaching staff to recognise the syndrome prevent unnecessary antipsychotic prescribing. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor for probable dementia with Lewy bodies and monitor closely
options.rationale: Dementia with Lewy bodies is the alternative cause of formed visual hallucinations in this age group, but it requires cognitive impairment and is supported by fluctuating attention, parkinsonism, falls or dream enactment, all of which are absent. Her cognition is intact and her insight is preserved, which is not the pattern of that disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

explanation.summary: Complex formed visual hallucinations occurring in a person with significant visual loss, with full insight and no other psychotic symptoms or cognitive decline, constitute Charles Bonnet syndrome. The mechanism is release activity in visual cortex deprived of input, and the images are characteristically vivid, detailed and often of people, faces, patterns or scenes. The main clinical task is recognition, because patients frequently conceal the symptom for fear of being thought mentally ill, and explanation alone relieves much of the distress. Management is conservative: optimise remaining vision, improve lighting and daytime stimulation, educate carers, and avoid antipsychotics, which carry substantial risk in older people and have little effect on these hallucinations.
key_points: Preserved insight with no other psychotic features distinguishes this from a psychotic disorder
Sustained attention and coherent account argue against delirium
Absent parkinsonism, fluctuation and cognitive decline argue against dementia with Lewy bodies
Explanation, vision optimisation and carer education replace antipsychotic prescribing
explanation.pearls: Ask any patient with severe visual loss whether they ever see things they know are not there, because most never volunteer it for fear of being thought mad. Vivid formed images with full insight and no cognitive decline is Charles Bonnet syndrome, and naming it to the patient and the aged care staff is more effective than any antipsychotic.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard
Vision Australia: Charles Bonnet syndrome information

subtopic_detail: depressive episodes recurring each winter with hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving that remit fully in spring
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who moved from Darwin to Hobart four years ago. Each year since, from late May, she has become flat, sleeps 10 to 11 hours and still feels unrefreshed, craves bread and sweet foods, gains about 5 kg, and withdraws from her netball team.

By early October she is back to her usual self, energetic and social, with the weight coming off without effort, and she stays well right through summer. This has now happened four winters in a row and has never happened at any other time of year. She works indoors in an office with no window. She denies elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or overspending at any time, and there is no alcohol or other substance misuse. Her thyroid function, full blood count, iron studies and vitamin D are all within normal limits, and she is currently five weeks into this year's episode with no suicidal ideation.

data_table.Symptom pattern: Four consecutive winters of low mood with hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and 5 kg weight gain, full remission each spring
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count, iron studies and vitamin D within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Low mood with reactivity preserved, no suicidal ideation, no history of elevated mood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for this episode?

options.text: Start lithium as a mood stabiliser given the regular recurrence of her mood episodes
options.rationale: Lithium is used for bipolar disorder and as augmentation in resistant depression, and its use here would require a history of elevated mood, which she clearly denies. Regularity of recurrence alone does not make a mood disorder bipolar. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Prescribe high dose oral vitamin D through winter and review her mood in eight weeks
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency is worth correcting when present, particularly in southern Australian winters, but her level is already normal and supplementation has not been shown to treat this pattern of depression. Choosing it would leave the episode untreated for another two months. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Begin bright light therapy each morning with structured behavioural activation alongside it
options.rationale: Daily morning exposure to a bright light source is an established first line treatment for depression with a seasonal pattern, with response usually apparent within one to two weeks, and it suits someone who works indoors without daylight. Pairing it with scheduled activity and re-engagement with her sport targets the withdrawal that maintains the episode. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy because the episodes have recurred for four consecutive years
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is reserved for severe depression with high risk features such as food refusal, psychosis or persistent suicidality, or for failure of multiple adequate treatments. A recurrent but moderate and fully remitting illness does not meet that threshold. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Advise watchful waiting until October, since her episodes have always resolved spontaneously
options.rationale: Predictable remission does not make four months of impairment each year acceptable, and untreated episodes carry occupational, social and suicide risk. The predictability is better used to plan treatment before the next episode starts. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: A seasonal pattern is specified when depressive episodes occur at a characteristic time of year with full remission at another, across at least two consecutive years and with seasonal episodes substantially outnumbering non-seasonal ones. The atypical features of hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving and weight gain are typical of the winter pattern, and the presentation is more common at higher latitudes, which in Australia means Tasmania and southern Victoria. Bright light therapy given in the morning is first line, generally producing a response within one to two weeks, and is often combined with behavioural activation. Antidepressants and psychological therapy remain effective options, and because the timing is predictable, treatment can be started before the expected onset in subsequent years.
key_points: Diagnosis requires the seasonal relationship across at least two consecutive years with full remission between
Hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain are the characteristic atypical features
Morning bright light therapy is first line, with response usually within one to two weeks
Predictable timing allows preventive treatment started before the expected onset next year
explanation.pearls: Once a seasonal pattern is established over two or more years, use the predictability: start morning bright light therapy in the fortnight before the usual onset next autumn rather than waiting five weeks into the episode, which is when most patients present.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic, Depression

subtopic_detail: patient request for a psychedelic assisted treatment after reading about its regulatory approval
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 46-year-old man with a 14 month depressive episode. He asks to be started on psilocybin assisted therapy, having read that it is now legally available in Australia for treatment resistant depression, and says he does not want to try another tablet.

His current episode has been treated with sertraline titrated to 200 mg daily for 10 weeks with partial response, then a switch to venlafaxine 225 mg daily for 9 weeks with no further improvement. He has had 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy. He has never had psychosis or mania, has no family history of bipolar disorder, drinks two standard drinks a week, and takes no other medication. He remains able to work part time and denies suicidal ideation. He asks you directly whether you can prescribe it for him at this appointment or whether he should buy it privately from an overseas supplier.

data_table.Treatment history: Sertraline 200 mg daily for 10 weeks with partial response, venlafaxine 225 mg daily for 9 weeks with no improvement, 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy
data_table.Risk: No suicidal ideation, no psychosis or mania, no family history of bipolar disorder
data_table.Substance use: Two standard drinks per week, no other substances

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to his request?

options.text: Prescribe psilocybin yourself today, since it is now approved for this indication in Australia
options.rationale: Access is restricted to psychiatrists who hold specific authorisation for this purpose and who deliver it within an approved protocol including preparation, supervised dosing and integration sessions. Prescribing outside that framework would breach the conditions under which access exists. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Access to psilocybin and MDMA)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Access to psilocybin and MDMA

options.text: Tell him that the treatment is unavailable in Australia and that overseas purchase is his only route
options.rationale: This is factually wrong, since a regulated pathway exists through authorised psychiatrists, and it would push a vulnerable patient toward an unregulated supply with no screening, no supervision and legal risk. Telling a patient something is unavailable when it is not damages trust as well as safety. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Access to psilocybin and MDMA)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Access to psilocybin and MDMA

options.text: Agree to supervise a session if he obtains the substance himself and brings it to the clinic
options.rationale: Supervising the use of an unregulated substance of unknown identity and purity provides none of the safeguards of an authorised programme and exposes both patient and practitioner to serious risk. Willingness to supervise does not make an unlawful supply safe. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances

options.text: Explain the authorised prescriber pathway and offer an evidence based next step meanwhile
options.rationale: The honest answer is that access exists but only through psychiatrists holding specific authorisation and within a structured protocol, and that referral to such a service takes time and involves cost and careful screening. Meanwhile he has not yet had augmentation, a third agent, or a trial of an established interventional treatment, so offering one of those keeps his depression treated while the referral proceeds. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances

options.text: Decline the discussion and restate that only a third antidepressant trial is acceptable now
options.rationale: Refusing to engage with a reasonable question about an approved treatment leaves him to seek information elsewhere and makes unsupervised use more likely. Recommending another antidepressant is defensible, but it should follow the conversation rather than replace it. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances

explanation.summary: Since mid 2023 psilocybin may be prescribed in Australia for treatment resistant depression, and MDMA for post traumatic stress disorder, but only by psychiatrists who hold authorised prescriber approval and who deliver the substance within a protocol of preparation, supervised dosing and integration. General prescribing, compounding at home and self sourced material all fall outside this framework. Screening excludes people with a personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder because of the risk of precipitating a psychotic or manic episode, and serotonergic antidepressants usually need to be tapered before dosing. The appropriate clinical response is to explain the pathway accurately, refer if the patient wishes to pursue it, and in the meantime continue evidence based treatment, which for this man has not yet included augmentation or an interventional option.
key_points: Access is restricted to authorised prescribers working within an approved protocol
Screening excludes personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder
Existing serotonergic antidepressants generally require tapering before dosing
Continue established treatment while any referral for this pathway is pursued
explanation.pearls: Answer the access question accurately rather than shutting it down: psilocybin for treatment resistant depression is lawful in Australia only through an authorised prescriber delivering preparation, supervised dosing and integration, and saying so while offering augmentation or an interventional option in the interim is what keeps a patient away from an overseas supplier.

subtopic_detail: loss of control over online gaming with withdrawal from school and sport over twelve months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old boy brought by his father, who is worried about the amount of time he spends gaming. Over the past 12 months his gaming has risen to eight or nine hours daily, mostly between 7 pm and 3 am.

He has quit the soccer team, stopped seeing friends in person, and his school attendance has fallen to about half the timetable, with grades dropping from mostly B to mostly D. He becomes verbally aggressive when the internet is switched off and has repeatedly promised to cut down and failed within days. He denies low mood when he is gaming but says everything else feels pointless, and he has no suicidal ideation on direct questioning. He eats irregularly, has lost 3 kg, is not using alcohol or other substances, and there is no history of trauma or bullying that either he or his father can identify.

data_table.Pattern: Eight to nine hours daily gaming mostly overnight for twelve months, repeated failed attempts to reduce, irritability when access is removed
data_table.Function: School attendance halved with falling grades, sport and in-person friendships abandoned, 3 kg weight loss
data_table.Mental state: No suicidal ideation, no substance use, denies low mood while gaming

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Assess for depression and other comorbidity, then refer for family based psychological therapy
options.rationale: Problem gaming of this severity is usually accompanied by depression, anxiety or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and treating a missed comorbidity changes the outcome more than addressing screen time alone. The intervention with the best support involves the family, since parents control access and the treatment plan has to include sleep, school re-engagement and graded reduction rather than abrupt confiscation. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

options.text: Advise the father to remove the console and the router permanently from the house tonight
options.rationale: Sudden total removal commonly escalates aggression and can precipitate absconding or self harm in an adolescent whose only social contact is online. Graded reduction negotiated with the young person is both safer and more durable. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

options.text: Start an antidepressant now, since withdrawal from activities indicates a depressive episode
options.rationale: Loss of interest in previously valued activities does suggest depression, but here it may be a consequence of the gaming pattern and the reversed sleep cycle rather than an independent disorder. Assessment should establish which is present before a medicine is started. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

options.text: Reassure the father that heavy gaming is normal at this age and recommend a screen time contract
options.rationale: Many adolescents game heavily without harm, which is exactly why the diagnostic threshold rests on impaired control plus functional damage, and halved school attendance with abandoned sport and friendships crosses it. A contract alone has already failed in the repeated attempts to cut down. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer him to a residential drug and alcohol rehabilitation programme for behavioural addiction
options.rationale: Residential programmes are designed around substance withdrawal and are not the established pathway for this problem, and removing him from school and family would worsen the functional losses. Outpatient psychological work with the family is the appropriate level of care. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Gaming disorder is defined by impaired control over gaming, increasing priority given to it over other interests and daily activities, and continuation despite negative consequences, with the pattern persisting for about 12 months and causing significant functional impairment. The threshold is functional harm rather than hours played, which is why halved school attendance, abandoned sport and lost in-person friendships matter more than the raw figure. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, so assessment for depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder comes first, along with sleep, since reversed sleep cycles both worsen and are worsened by overnight gaming. Management is psychological and family based, working toward graded reduction, restored sleep and school re-engagement, since abrupt total removal of access commonly escalates conflict without producing durable change.
key_points: Functional impairment, not hours played, defines the disorder
Screen for depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder before attributing everything to gaming
Family based psychological therapy with graded reduction is the mainstay
Abrupt total removal of access commonly escalates aggression and risk
explanation.pearls: Ask what the gaming has cost rather than how many hours it takes: school attendance, sport and face to face friendships are the ledger that distinguishes a disorder from an ordinary adolescent hobby, and the first move is screening for depression and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder before any screen time plan.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents
RCH CPG: Adolescent mental health assessment

subtopic_detail: belief that a spouse has been replaced by an identical impostor in a man with fluctuating cognition
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 76-year-old man at home with his wife of 50 years. For three months he has insisted that she is not his real wife but an identical looking substitute, and he has twice asked her to leave the house at night, though he accepts her cooking and sits with her during the day.

His wife reports that his attention comes and goes, with some days lucid and others where he stares and is hard to rouse into conversation. He has seen small animals in the lounge room for over a year. He has acted out dreams and fallen out of bed several times, and he has become slower with a stooped posture and a mild resting tremor of the left hand over the past year. Screening bloods including full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, B12 and urinalysis are all normal. He takes no anticholinergic medication and there has been no recent change to any prescription.

data_table.Examination: Stooped posture, reduced arm swing, mild left resting tremor, attention fluctuating markedly through the interview
data_table.History: Formed visual hallucinations for more than a year, dream enactment with falls from bed, three months of misidentification of his wife
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and urinalysis all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the misidentification?

options.text: Start haloperidol 0.5 mg at night, titrating upward until the belief about his wife resolves
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics can provoke severe sensitivity reactions in this condition, with marked rigidity, immobility, autonomic instability and increased mortality, and haloperidol is the agent most associated with it. This is the single most dangerous choice in an older person with this constellation. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Arrange urgent admission for a delirium screen and intravenous fluids with regular orientation
options.rationale: Fluctuating attention genuinely raises delirium, and it would be the priority if this had developed over days with an identifiable precipitant, but the course here spans a year with a stable medication list and normal screening tests. Admitting him would remove the familiar environment that currently keeps him settled. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Advise his wife to correct him firmly each time and to show him their wedding photographs
options.rationale: Direct confrontation of a fixed misidentification typically increases agitation and can escalate to aggression, and it places the person he does not recognise at the centre of the dispute. Practical strategies such as approaching from the front, announcing herself by voice, and stepping away and re-entering are more effective. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Begin a cholinesterase inhibitor with carer strategies and a documented night time safety plan
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are the preferred first line for psychotic and cognitive symptoms in this disorder, with better evidence and far less risk than antipsychotics, and they often reduce hallucinations and misidentification over weeks. Coupling this with carer strategies for approach and reorientation, and an explicit plan for what his wife does if he asks her to leave at night, manages the risk while the medication takes effect. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Commence levodopa to treat the parkinsonian features and reassess the psychotic symptoms after
options.rationale: Dopaminergic therapy may be needed for disabling motor symptoms but characteristically worsens hallucinations and delusions in this condition, so it is the wrong lever when psychosis is the presenting problem. If it becomes necessary, it is introduced cautiously at the lowest effective dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Parkinson disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Parkinson disease

explanation.summary: The belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor is a delusional misidentification syndrome, and in an older person it most often occurs within dementia with Lewy bodies. The supporting features here are the full core set: fluctuating cognition and attention, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, dream enactment behaviour, and spontaneous parkinsonism. Antipsychotics carry a serious sensitivity risk in this disorder, with rigidity, immobility, autonomic instability and increased mortality, and typical agents are the most hazardous. Cholinesterase inhibitors are therefore first line for the neuropsychiatric symptoms, combined with carer strategies and an explicit safety plan, with quetiapine at low dose reserved for severe distress or risk that does not respond.
key_points: Misidentification of a spouse in an older person points to a neurodegenerative rather than primary psychotic cause
Fluctuation, visual hallucinations, dream enactment and parkinsonism form the core diagnostic cluster
Antipsychotic sensitivity in this disorder can be severe and is worst with typical agents
Cholinesterase inhibitors plus carer strategies are first line for the psychotic symptoms
explanation.pearls: Before prescribing any antipsychotic to an older person with new delusions, ask the partner whether he acts out his dreams and whether his alertness varies from day to day. Dream enactment with fluctuation and visual hallucinations signals antipsychotic sensitivity, and a cholinesterase inhibitor with carer strategies replaces the prescription you were about to write.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people
Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Parkinson disease
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

subtopic_detail: colleague smelling of alcohol before a ward round after repeated concerns raised by nursing staff
stem:
You are a psychiatry registrar. Before the morning ward round you notice that the consultant you are working with smells strongly of alcohol, has a tremor, and is slurring occasional words. Two nurses tell you privately that they noticed the same thing twice last week.

He is due to lead a round on 18 inpatients and to review three people detained under mental health legislation, including decisions about leave. When you speak to him quietly he says he had a late night, denies drinking this morning, and becomes irritable, telling you to mind your own business and that he is perfectly fine to work. He has not had any formal performance concerns raised in the past to your knowledge. There is no immediate patient harm that has occurred yet today, and the round has not started. You are not his supervisor and there is no other consultant currently on the ward.

data_table.Observed findings: Strong smell of alcohol, tremor, intermittent slurred speech before a ward round
data_table.Corroboration: Two nursing staff independently report the same observation on two occasions last week
data_table.Clinical exposure: Ward round of 18 inpatients including three detained patients with leave decisions pending
data_table.Response to approach: Denies drinking this morning, becomes irritable, declines to step back

lead_in: What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing further today and raise it with him privately again after the ward round has finished
options.rationale: Waiting until after the round allows an impaired practitioner to make detention and leave decisions for 18 patients, which is exactly the harm the reporting framework exists to prevent. A conversation after the fact cannot undo decisions already made. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Escalate immediately to the on call senior so the round is covered, then make a notification
options.rationale: The immediate patient safety step is to ensure the round is conducted by someone fit to practise, which means escalating now to the medical administrator or on call senior rather than negotiating with the colleague. Practising while intoxicated by alcohol meets the threshold for notifiable conduct, so a notification follows, and the two obligations run in parallel rather than as alternatives. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Ask the nursing staff to document their concerns and submit an incident report at the end of the week
options.rationale: Documentation matters, but an incident report filed at the end of the week does not remove an impaired doctor from patient care this morning. Delegating the response to nursing staff also shifts a responsibility that is personally yours once you hold a reasonable belief. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Offer to lead the round yourself while he rests, and keep the matter between the two of you
options.rationale: Covering for a colleague protects today's patients but conceals a pattern that has already been observed twice by others and leaves him untreated and still rostered. Informal accommodation of impairment is the commonest way these situations continue for years. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Arrange a blood alcohol level and proceed only if the result confirms recent alcohol consumption
options.rationale: You have no authority to require testing of a colleague, and the obligation to act is triggered by a reasonable belief formed on observation rather than by laboratory proof. Insisting on a test would delay the response while the round proceeds. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

explanation.summary: Registered health practitioners in Australia have a mandatory obligation to notify when they form a reasonable belief that another practitioner has practised while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs, engaged in sexual misconduct, placed the public at substantial risk through an impairment, or departed significantly from accepted standards. A reasonable belief rests on direct observation and corroborating information rather than proof, so no test result is required before acting. Two obligations operate at once: securing immediate patient safety by escalating so that someone fit to practise covers the clinical work, and making the notification. Treating practitioners have modified obligations in most jurisdictions, which is designed to encourage doctors to seek help for their own health, and support services for practitioners with substance use problems exist alongside the regulatory pathway.
key_points: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is notifiable conduct, not a matter for private accommodation
A reasonable belief formed on observation is the trigger; laboratory confirmation is not required
Secure immediate patient safety by escalating for cover, then notify; the steps run in parallel
Practitioner health services support the colleague alongside the regulatory process
explanation.pearls: Two things happen at once when a colleague is impaired at work: someone fit to practise must take over the clinical load right now, and the notification follows. Waiting for a blood alcohol level or for the end of the round converts a reasonable belief into a delayed one while patients are still being seen.

sources.label: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications
Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice, a code of conduct

subtopic_detail: early script requests and a negative urine screen in a young adult prescribed stimulant medication
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 23-year-old man diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder 18 months ago and prescribed dexamfetamine. He has requested early replacement scripts three times in five months, citing a lost bottle, a spilled bottle and a bag stolen at a music festival.

He reports that the medication works well and that he has no side effects. His flatmate telephoned the clinic last month to ask whether the tablets could be bought. A urine drug screen collected at the last visit, two days after he said he had taken his morning dose, detected no amphetamine. His weight is stable, his blood pressure is normal, and he is in his third year of an engineering degree with passing grades. He appears well, is not agitated, and there are no signs of intoxication or withdrawal, no injection marks and no reported alcohol or other substance use.

data_table.Prescribing history: Three early replacement script requests in five months with differing explanations
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamine two days after a reported dose, weight stable
data_table.Collateral: Flatmate telephoned the clinic asking whether the tablets could be purchased

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Issue the replacement script and arrange a pharmacy owed-medication record for future losses
options.rationale: Continuing to replace without addressing the negative screen ignores evidence that the medication is not reaching the patient, and an administrative record does not alter diversion. Prescribing on the same pattern is what allows it to continue. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

options.text: Report him to police for suspected supply and cease all prescribing without further discussion
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation without discussion abandons a patient who may have a genuine disorder and severs the relationship in which the problem can actually be addressed. Suspicion of diversion is managed clinically and through the prescription monitoring system, not by an unsupported criminal allegation. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

options.text: Double the dose, on the basis that the negative screen indicates inadequate absorption of the drug
options.rationale: A negative screen two days after a reported dose points to the medication not being taken rather than to a pharmacokinetic problem, and dexamfetamine is reliably detectable in urine for one to three days after ingestion. Increasing the supply would place more of a diverted drug in circulation. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

options.text: Check the real time prescription monitoring system, discuss the findings openly, and revise the plan
options.rationale: The monitoring system shows whether other prescribers and pharmacies are involved and converts suspicion into fact before any decision is made, and the conversation that follows is what preserves the therapeutic relationship. Where the findings support diversion, the plan moves toward staged supply, more frequent review, or a switch to a non-stimulant agent. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

options.text: Switch immediately to atomoxetine without discussing the screen result or the script requests
options.rationale: A non-stimulant agent is a reasonable destination and removes the diversion risk, but changing treatment without naming the reason denies the patient the chance to explain and leaves the underlying situation unexamined. The conversation has to precede the switch. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

explanation.summary: Repeated early script requests with varying explanations, a third party asking to buy the medication, and a urine screen negative for the prescribed stimulant together suggest diversion rather than a dosing problem. Real time prescription monitoring, available across Australian jurisdictions, establishes whether other prescribers or pharmacies are supplying the same drug and turns a suspicion into documented fact before any decision is made. The clinical response is to discuss the findings openly, since a defensible plan requires the patient's account, and then to revise prescribing toward staged or weekly dispensing, more frequent review, or a non-stimulant agent such as atomoxetine or guanfacine. Abrupt cessation without discussion and continued unexamined prescribing are both failures, in opposite directions.
key_points: A urine screen negative for the prescribed stimulant is strong evidence the drug is not being taken
Real time prescription monitoring establishes multiple prescriber or pharmacy involvement
Discuss the findings with the patient before changing or ceasing treatment
Staged supply, closer review, or a non-stimulant agent are the usual revisions to the plan
explanation.pearls: A urine drug screen that is negative for the very stimulant you prescribed, taken within two days of a reported dose, is the finding that should stop the next script: check real time prescription monitoring first, then have the conversation, then move to staged supply or a non-stimulant agent.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic, Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

subtopic_detail: severe irritability and despair confined to the week before menstruation with complete resolution by day three
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman who describes becoming, in her words, a different person for about six days before each period. She is irritable to the point of shouting at her children, feels hopeless, cannot concentrate at work, and has cancelled social plans repeatedly.

By the third day of bleeding she feels entirely well again and stays well for the rest of the month. She has kept a daily symptom chart for three consecutive cycles at her previous doctor's suggestion, and it shows the symptoms confined to the luteal phase with symptom free scores from day three through to day 18 in every cycle. Her thyroid function and full blood count are normal. She has never had a depressive episode outside this pattern, drinks alcohol rarely, does not use contraception and does not plan a pregnancy this year, and there is no suicidal ideation now or during the symptomatic phase.

data_table.Symptom chart: Three consecutive cycles charted with symptoms confined to the six days before menstruation and complete resolution by day three of bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.History: No depressive episodes outside the luteal phase, no suicidal ideation, no pregnancy planned this year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe calcium and vitamin B6 supplementation and review the charts after three cycles
options.rationale: Calcium supplementation has modest evidence for milder premenstrual symptoms and vitamin B6 is widely used, so both are reasonable adjuncts for mild cases. Neither matches the effect size of the first line pharmacological option in a woman whose symptoms are severe enough to disrupt work and parenting. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer for a gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist with added back hormonal therapy
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is highly effective and is used when first and second line treatments fail, but it induces a menopausal state requiring add-back therapy and bone monitoring. It is a specialist option reserved for refractory disease, not a starting point. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders

options.text: Start a serotonergic antidepressant given either continuously or in the luteal phase only
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line for this disorder and are unusual in working within a day or two rather than over weeks, which is what makes luteal phase dosing from ovulation until menstruation a genuine alternative to continuous treatment. The choice between the two schedules is made with the woman, weighing cycle predictability and tolerability against the simplicity of taking it every day. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Begin lithium at a low dose, treating this as a rapid cycling presentation of a bipolar disorder
options.rationale: Rapid cycling requires four or more mood episodes in a year meeting full criteria for depressive, manic or hypomanic episodes, and she has no elevated mood at any point. Symptoms tied to the luteal phase and resolving with menstruation are not mood episodes in that sense. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Advise aerobic exercise and sleep hygiene alone, with review only if the symptoms worsen further
options.rationale: Exercise and sleep measures help and should be part of the plan, but offered alone they are inadequate for symptoms that are already causing her to shout at her children and cancel commitments each month. Withholding effective treatment until things worsen is not a defensible threshold. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is diagnosed from prospective daily symptom ratings across at least two cycles showing affective and physical symptoms confined to the final week before menstruation, improving within a few days of onset of bleeding and absent in the week after. Retrospective recall is unreliable, which is why the charting requirement is part of the diagnosis rather than an optional extra. Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line and act within a day or two in this condition, so they can be taken continuously or only from ovulation until menstruation begins, with similar efficacy. Combined hormonal contraception taken continuously is an alternative, particularly when contraception is also wanted, and ovarian suppression with add-back therapy is reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: Prospective daily charting over at least two cycles is required for the diagnosis
Symptoms must resolve within days of menstruation starting and be absent mid cycle
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors work within days here, allowing luteal phase only dosing
Ovarian suppression with add-back therapy is reserved for refractory disease
explanation.pearls: The rapid onset of benefit is what makes this disorder different from depression: a serotonin reuptake inhibitor works within a day or two, so it can be taken only from ovulation until bleeding starts, which many women prefer to daily dosing for a problem confined to one week in four.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic, Premenstrual dysphoric disorder

subtopic_detail: escalating self directed dose increases of a gabapentinoid with euphoria and early script exhaustion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old man who was prescribed pregabalin 150 mg twice daily for neuropathic pain after a work injury nine months ago. He asks for an early script for the third month running.

He tells you that he has been taking up to 1200 mg a day because the usual dose stopped helping, and that at the higher doses he feels relaxed and euphoric for a few hours. He has bought extra capsules from a friend twice. He drinks four to six standard drinks on most evenings, which he says helps the effect last. He is not injecting anything, has no opioid prescription, and denies stimulant use. His original pain has largely settled and his back examination today is normal, with no new neurological signs. He says he feels sweaty and anxious if he goes a day without taking any.

data_table.Medication use: Prescribed 300 mg daily, taking up to 1200 mg daily, purchasing additional capsules, early script requests three months running
data_table.Other substance use: Four to six standard drinks most evenings, no opioids, no injecting drug use
data_table.Examination: Back examination normal with no new neurological signs, original neuropathic pain largely resolved

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Plan a structured taper with staged dispensing, and address the alcohol use at the same time
options.rationale: He has developed tolerance, dose escalation, craving and autonomic symptoms on missed doses, so abrupt cessation risks a withdrawal syndrome while unchanged prescribing sustains the problem, leaving a gradual planned reduction as the safe route. Staged dispensing limits the quantity on hand, and the concurrent alcohol use must be addressed because the combination markedly increases the risk of respiratory depression and fatal overdose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse

options.text: Stop the pregabalin immediately today and provide a letter explaining the decision to him
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal from high dose gabapentinoids can produce agitation, insomnia, sweating, tachycardia and occasionally seizures, particularly alongside heavy alcohol use. Sudden cessation also predictably drives purchase from unregulated sources. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse

options.text: Increase the prescribed dose to 600 mg twice daily so that he stops buying from other sources
options.rationale: Prescribing to match a self escalated dose legitimises tolerance driven escalation and raises the overdose risk, especially with nightly alcohol. Supply from other sources typically continues rather than stopping. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse

options.text: Switch him to a slow release opioid to manage the pain and avoid a withdrawal reaction
options.rationale: His pain has largely resolved and there is no indication for an opioid, which would add a second dependence-forming drug and compound the respiratory depression risk already created by alcohol. Substituting one problematic agent for a more dangerous one is not harm reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic, Chronic non-cancer pain)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic, Chronic non-cancer pain

options.text: Refer to a pain clinic and continue the current prescription unchanged until he is seen there
options.rationale: Multidisciplinary pain input is valuable, but waiting lists run to months and the prescribing problem is active now, with purchasing from a friend and daily heavy alcohol use. Continuing unchanged defers the decision that this consultation exists to make. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse

explanation.summary: Pregabalin misuse has risen substantially in Australia and is characterised by self directed dose escalation, euphoria at supratherapeutic doses, sourcing from outside the prescription, and withdrawal symptoms on missed doses. The risk is greatest in combination with alcohol, opioids or benzodiazepines, since the combination is strongly associated with fatal respiratory depression, and pregabalin now features frequently in Australian overdose deaths. Abrupt cessation risks a withdrawal syndrome that can include seizures, so management is a planned taper with staged dispensing, review of the original indication, and concurrent treatment of the alcohol use. Real time prescription monitoring supports the plan by identifying additional prescribers.
key_points: Dose escalation, euphoria and sourcing outside the prescription define gabapentinoid misuse
Combination with alcohol or opioids drives the fatal respiratory depression risk
Abrupt cessation can precipitate withdrawal including seizures, so taper rather than stop
Staged dispensing and prescription monitoring support the taper plan
explanation.pearls: Ask what the patient drinks in the evening before deciding what to do about a gabapentinoid script: pregabalin with nightly alcohol is the combination that turns up in Australian overdose deaths, and the plan is a structured taper with staged dispensing plus treatment of the alcohol, never an abrupt stop.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse
Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic, Chronic non-cancer pain
NPS MedicineWise: Pregabalin safety

subtopic_detail: wet season community acquired pneumonia in a diabetic gardener in the tropical north with rapid deterioration
stem:
You are the medical registrar in Darwin in February. A 54-year-old man is admitted with four days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain, having deteriorated over the past 12 hours.

He has type 2 diabetes with a glycated haemoglobin of 9.8 per cent, drinks heavily, and spent last weekend digging drainage channels in mud around his property after heavy rain. He has not travelled outside the Northern Territory. Chest radiograph shows a right upper lobe consolidation with a small cavity. Blood cultures taken on arrival are flagged at six hours as growing a Gram negative bacillus with bipolar staining described by the laboratory as having a safety pin appearance. He was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin in the emergency department four hours ago and has since required 6 litres of oxygen by mask, with worsening tachypnoea and hypotension.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 91% on 6 litres per minute, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glycated haemoglobin 9.8 per cent
data_table.Imaging: Right upper lobe consolidation with a small cavity
data_table.Microbiology: Blood cultures growing a Gram negative bacillus with bipolar safety pin staining at six hours

lead_in: What antibiotic change should you make now?

options.text: Add vancomycin to cover methicillin resistant staphylococcal cavitating pneumonia
options.rationale: Staphylococcal pneumonia does cavitate and is worth considering in this setting, but the organism in the blood is a Gram negative bacillus, which excludes it. Adding glycopeptide cover would leave the actual pathogen inadequately treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis

options.text: Change to intravenous meropenem, with trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole considered for eradication
options.rationale: Bipolar safety pin staining of a Gram negative bacillus in a diabetic man exposed to wet soil in the tropical north during the wet season indicates melioidosis, which is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone and gentamicin. Intensive therapy uses meropenem in severe disease or in those with septic shock, followed by months of oral eradication therapy to prevent relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis

options.text: Continue ceftriaxone and azithromycin and add oseltamivir for possible influenza co-infection
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone does not reliably treat this organism, which is one of the classic reasons that patients in the tropical north deteriorate on standard community acquired pneumonia therapy. Antiviral therapy addresses a different pathogen entirely and does not explain a Gram negative bacteraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis

options.text: Switch to intravenous benzylpenicillin with doxycycline for atypical and zoonotic pathogens
options.rationale: This combination covers leptospirosis and rickettsial infection, which are reasonable wet season considerations in northern Australia, but neither produces a Gram negative bacillus with this staining pattern. Narrowing to penicillin in septic shock from this organism would be dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis

options.text: Add intravenous metronidazole for anaerobic cover given the cavitating upper lobe lesion
options.rationale: Anaerobic cover is appropriate for aspiration associated cavitation, which fits his alcohol use, but an aspiration process would not produce this blood culture result. Adding metronidazole leaves the identified organism untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by an environmental Gram negative bacillus found in soil and surface water across northern Australia, and cases cluster in the wet season after exposure to mud and heavy rain. The major risk factors are diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, chronic lung or kidney disease, and immunosuppression, and presentations range from pneumonia, often cavitating, to abscesses and septic shock. The organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, ceftriaxone and aminoglycosides, so patients characteristically deteriorate on standard community acquired pneumonia therapy while the culture is incubating. Treatment has two phases: intensive intravenous therapy with meropenem for severe disease or ceftazidime for less severe disease, for at least two weeks, followed by three months of oral eradication therapy, usually trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, because relapse is otherwise common.
key_points: Wet season soil exposure with diabetes or heavy alcohol use is the classic risk profile in northern Australia
The organism is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone, penicillins and aminoglycosides
Severe disease or septic shock is treated with meropenem rather than ceftazidime
Oral eradication therapy for about three months is required to prevent relapse
explanation.pearls: A patient in the tropical north who is deteriorating on ceftriaxone for pneumonia after wet season soil exposure has melioidosis until the cultures say otherwise: switch to meropenem for severe disease and plan three months of oral eradication therapy, because stopping at the intravenous phase is what produces relapse.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis
CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Melioidosis
