subtopic_detail: coagulopathy after a suspected snake bite with a normal bite site and no systemic symptoms
stem:
You are the doctor at a rural emergency department in western New South Wales. A 41-year-old man arrives 90 minutes after feeling something strike his ankle while moving hay bales. He did not see the animal clearly.

A pressure immobilisation bandage was applied by his wife over the whole limb and splinted, and it remains in place. He feels well, with no headache, no vomiting, no abdominal pain, no ptosis and no weakness. There are two faint scratches on the lateral ankle with no swelling, no bruising and no local pain. Point of care testing and formal laboratory results have returned. Antivenom is available in the department, and the nearest tertiary centre with intensive care is a 2 hour road transfer or a 40 minute flight, with the retrieval service contactable. He has no medical history, takes no anticoagulant and has never received antivenom.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Two faint scratches on the lateral ankle without swelling or bruising, pressure immobilisation bandage and splint in place, no ptosis or limb weakness
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio greater than 12, activated partial thromboplastin time greater than 180 seconds, fibrinogen not detected, D-dimer markedly elevated, creatine kinase 180 U/L (40-200), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Logistics: Antivenom stocked on site, retrieval service contactable, tertiary centre two hours by road

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Remove the bandage and observe for six hours, repeating coagulation studies before any treatment
options.rationale: The coagulation results already establish systemic envenoming, so there is nothing further to observe for before treating, and removing the bandage before antivenom is drawn up allows a further bolus of venom to enter the circulation. Serial testing is used to follow recovery after antivenom, not to decide whether to give it. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate now to correct the undetectable fibrinogen
options.rationale: Factor replacement without antivenom is consumed by circulating venom and does not correct the coagulopathy, so it is given only after antivenom and generally only when there is significant bleeding or a need for an urgent procedure. Treating the laboratory result rather than the envenoming wastes time and product. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

options.text: Perform a venom detection kit test on the bite site and withhold treatment until the result
options.rationale: The detection kit guides antivenom selection where the snake group is uncertain and multiple monovalent products are stocked, but it never determines whether to treat and its result should not delay antivenom in a patient with established coagulopathy. In much of Australia geography predicts the likely group well enough to proceed. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

options.text: Give one vial of antivenom intravenously with adrenaline prepared, keeping the bandage on until it runs
options.rationale: Undetectable fibrinogen with an unrecordable international normalised ratio is venom induced consumption coagulopathy, which is systemic envenoming and mandates antivenom regardless of how unimpressive the bite site looks or how well the patient feels. Australian evidence supports a single vial as the initial dose, given with adrenaline drawn up for anaphylaxis, and the pressure bandage stays in place until the infusion is running. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

options.text: Arrange immediate retrieval to the tertiary centre and defer antivenom until arrival there
options.rationale: Antivenom is stocked in this department and delaying it for a two hour transfer allows further venom mediated consumption and the risk of collapse or intracranial haemorrhage in transit. Retrieval is arranged in parallel with treatment, not instead of it. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

explanation.summary: Australian elapid envenoming is diagnosed on laboratory and clinical criteria rather than on the appearance of the bite, which is frequently trivial or invisible, and brown snakes in particular often cause severe coagulopathy with almost no local signs. Venom induced consumption coagulopathy, shown here by an unrecordable international normalised ratio with undetectable fibrinogen, is systemic envenoming and is the indication for antivenom. Australian data support a single vial as the initial dose, since larger doses do not improve outcome, given with adrenaline immediately available because anaphylaxis to antivenom is the main hazard. The pressure immobilisation bandage stays on until antivenom is running, factor replacement is reserved for bleeding or urgent procedures after antivenom, and coagulation studies are then repeated serially since recovery of fibrinogen typically takes many hours.
key_points: A trivial or absent bite site does not exclude severe systemic envenoming
Venom induced consumption coagulopathy is itself the indication for antivenom
One vial is the initial dose, with adrenaline prepared for anaphylaxis
Keep the pressure immobilisation bandage on until antivenom is running
explanation.pearls: Treat the coagulation profile, not the puncture marks: an unrecordable international normalised ratio with undetectable fibrinogen after a suspected snake bite is systemic envenoming, and one vial of the appropriate antivenom goes in before the pressure bandage comes off, with adrenaline drawn up at the bedside.

sources.label: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology, Snakebite

subtopic_detail: recurrent night time anaphylaxis several hours after meals in a bushwalker with frequent tick exposure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old man who has had three episodes in four months of generalised hives, lip swelling and wheeze, each waking him between 1 am and 3 am. Two required ambulance attendance and intramuscular adrenaline.

He lives on bushland on the New South Wales north coast and has had many tick bites, with several large local reactions. Each episode followed an evening meal by four to six hours. He has eaten fish, prawns and peanuts on other evenings with no problem at all. Reviewing the three meals with him, they were a beef stir fry, a lamb roast, and pork sausages, and he had no alcohol and took no medication in the hours before any episode, with no exercise beforehand. Skin prick testing to a standard food panel including peanut, shellfish, egg, milk and wheat is negative, and he has no history of asthma.

data_table.Episode pattern: Three nocturnal episodes of urticaria, angioedema and wheeze, each four to six hours after an evening meal, two treated with intramuscular adrenaline
data_table.Dietary review: Episodes followed beef, lamb and pork meals; fish, prawns and peanuts eaten uneventfully on other evenings
data_table.Exposure: Bushland residence with numerous tick bites and several large local reactions
data_table.Investigations: Skin prick testing to a standard food panel negative

lead_in: Which investigation will best confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Serum tryptase measured at baseline and again during a subsequent acute episode
options.rationale: Tryptase confirms that mast cell degranulation occurred and a persistently raised baseline would point toward a clonal mast cell disorder, but it identifies no trigger. It is a useful adjunct rather than the test that explains this pattern. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)
source_refs: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy

options.text: A supervised oral food challenge with beef performed in a hospital day unit
options.rationale: Challenge is hazardous when the reactions have been anaphylactic and the delayed timing makes the observation period impractical, running to six hours or more after ingestion. It is not the first line test when a specific serological marker exists. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)
source_refs: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy

options.text: A 24 hour urinary collection for methylhistamine and prostaglandin metabolites
options.rationale: Urinary mediator metabolites are used in the assessment of suspected mast cell disorders, particularly where flushing and diarrhoea dominate. They neither identify an allergen nor distinguish an allergic from a non-allergic mast cell process. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)
source_refs: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy

options.text: Patch testing to a meat panel read at 48 and 96 hours after application to the back
options.rationale: Patch testing detects delayed cell mediated contact hypersensitivity of the skin, a different mechanism from the immediate antibody mediated reaction underlying urticaria, angioedema and wheeze. The delay in this syndrome comes from digestion and absorption, not from a cell mediated response. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)
source_refs: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy

options.text: Specific immunoglobulin E to the carbohydrate galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose in serum
options.rationale: Delayed anaphylaxis several hours after beef, lamb or pork in someone with heavy tick exposure is mammalian meat allergy, in which sensitisation to a mammalian carbohydrate occurs through tick bites and the delay reflects the time taken for the allergen to be processed and absorbed in lipid particles. Serum specific immunoglobulin E to that carbohydrate is the confirmatory test, since standard skin prick panels do not contain it. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)
source_refs: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy

explanation.summary: Mammalian meat allergy is a tick induced sensitisation to a carbohydrate present in beef, lamb, pork and other mammalian meats but absent from fish, poultry and primates. It is well recognised along the eastern seaboard of Australia, particularly the New South Wales north coast and Sydney northern beaches, where the paralysis tick is endemic. The hallmark is delayed anaphylaxis, typically two to six hours after a meal, which frequently wakes the patient at night and is often misclassified as idiopathic because the timing breaks the expected immediate pattern and standard skin prick panels do not include the allergen. Diagnosis is by serum specific immunoglobulin E to the carbohydrate, and management combines avoidance of mammalian meat and related products, an adrenaline autoinjector with an action plan, and instruction in correct tick removal, since further bites sustain the sensitisation.
key_points: The delay of two to six hours after the meal is the feature that identifies this syndrome
Sensitisation follows tick bites and involves a carbohydrate absent from fish and poultry
Standard skin prick food panels do not contain the allergen, so negative testing is expected
Management includes avoidance, an adrenaline autoinjector, and correct tick removal advice
explanation.pearls: Anaphylaxis that wakes someone in the early hours is a dietary history question about the evening meal, not an idiopathic label: beef, lamb or pork four to six hours earlier in a tick exposed patient on the eastern seaboard calls for specific immunoglobulin E to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose, which the standard skin prick panel will never show.

sources.label: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy
ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: progressive exertional breathlessness in a benchtop fabricator with upper zone nodularity on imaging
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar. A 36-year-old man is referred with 10 months of progressive breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. He has cut and polished engineered stone kitchen benchtops for nine years, mostly dry cutting in an enclosed workshop with an ordinary dust mask.

He has never smoked and has no pets or birds, no mouldy workplace, no hot tub and no occupational exposure to hay or grain. He takes no medication and has no reflux, no joint symptoms, no rash and no Raynaud phenomenon. Examination reveals fine inspiratory crackles at both upper zones with no clubbing and no lymphadenopathy. High resolution computed tomography shows numerous small centrilobular and subpleural nodules in an upper zone predominant distribution with early conglomerate masses, and enlarged hilar nodes with peripheral calcification. Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern with a reduced transfer factor, and an interferon gamma release assay is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96% at rest falling to 89% after a six minute walk, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Occupational history: Nine years dry cutting and polishing engineered stone benchtops in an enclosed workshop with an ordinary dust mask
data_table.Imaging: Upper zone predominant centrilobular and subpleural nodules with early conglomerate masses, hilar nodes with peripheral calcification
data_table.Lung function: Restrictive spirometry with reduced transfer factor, interferon gamma release assay negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Remove him from further dust exposure, notify the work health authority, and screen for complications
options.rationale: The only intervention that alters the course of this disease is stopping exposure, and because it is a notifiable occupational condition in Australian jurisdictions the notification also triggers workplace inspection and screening of his coworkers. Ongoing surveillance is needed for the recognised complications, which include tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, chronic kidney disease and lung cancer, and he should be referred for compensation assessment. (Source: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica

options.text: Start oral prednisolone at 0.5 mg per kg daily and review the transfer factor in three months
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no established role in this disease and expose him to metabolic and infective complications, including reactivation of latent mycobacterial infection to which he is already predisposed. They are used for hypersensitivity pneumonitis or sarcoidosis, neither of which fits this exposure and imaging pattern. (Source: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica

options.text: Begin antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib on the basis of the restrictive pattern and crackles
options.rationale: Antifibrotics are approved for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and for progressive pulmonary fibrosis of other causes, a decision made after exposure control and multidisciplinary assessment rather than at first presentation. An upper zone nodular pattern in a young never-smoker is not the basal reticulation that drives that decision. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources

options.text: Treat empirically for tuberculosis with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol
options.rationale: This condition substantially increases the risk of tuberculosis and screening is part of follow up, but the interferon gamma release assay is negative and there are no constitutional symptoms or cavitation. Empirical quadruple therapy would expose him to significant toxicity without evidence of infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Tuberculosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Tuberculosis

options.text: Arrange surgical lung biopsy to establish the histological pattern before any further action
options.rationale: The exposure history and characteristic imaging make the diagnosis without tissue, and biopsy carries real morbidity in a man with a reduced transfer factor. It is reserved for cases where the pattern or the exposure history genuinely does not fit. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources

explanation.summary: Engineered stone contains a far higher proportion of crystalline silica than natural stone, and dry cutting in poorly ventilated workshops produced an epidemic of accelerated silicosis in young Australian benchtop workers, leading to a national prohibition on the fabrication of engineered stone from mid 2024. The clinical picture is progressive breathlessness in a young never-smoker with upper zone predominant nodules, conglomerate masses and hilar nodes that may calcify peripherally. There is no disease modifying drug treatment, so the priorities are complete removal from exposure, notification so that the workplace is inspected and coworkers screened, and referral for compensation. Long term surveillance covers tuberculosis, autoimmune connective tissue disease, chronic kidney disease and lung cancer, with transplantation considered for end stage disease.
key_points: Engineered stone dry cutting causes accelerated disease after only a few years of exposure
Upper zone nodularity with conglomerate masses in a young never-smoker is the characteristic pattern
Exposure removal and notification are the interventions that change outcomes
Screen long term for tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, renal impairment and lung cancer
explanation.pearls: Ask what a young breathless never-smoker does for work before ordering anything: nine years of dry cutting engineered stone benchtops makes silicosis the diagnosis on imaging alone, and the treatment is permanent removal from dust plus notification to the work health authority so that the whole workshop is screened.

sources.label: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica
Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Tuberculosis

subtopic_detail: facial swelling and distended chest wall veins worse on bending forward with a right hilar mass
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department. A 62-year-old woman with a 40 pack year smoking history describes three weeks of facial puffiness that is worst on waking, and a sensation of fullness in her head when she bends to tie her shoes.

She has noticed her rings are tight and that her voice has become slightly hoarse. On examination the face and both arms are swollen with dilated veins visible across the upper chest wall, and the jugular venous pulsation is not visible because the veins are distended without pulsation. She has no stridor, speaks in full sentences, and her conscious state is normal with no headache, no confusion and no visual disturbance. Chest radiograph shows a right hilar mass with widening of the superior mediastinum. She has had no previous cancer diagnosis, no indwelling central venous catheter and no pacemaker, and she is not anticoagulated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Facial and bilateral arm swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins, dilated chest wall collateral veins, no stridor, normal conscious state
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph showing a right hilar mass with superior mediastinal widening
data_table.History: 40 pack year smoking history, no previous malignancy, no central venous catheter or pacemaker

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start high dose dexamethasone and arrange urgent mediastinal radiotherapy before any biopsy
options.rationale: Radiotherapy given before tissue is obtained can make subsequent histology uninterpretable and may preclude the diagnosis of a chemosensitive tumour such as lymphoma or small cell carcinoma, which would be treated quite differently. Immediate radiotherapy without tissue is reserved for genuine airway compromise or neurological deterioration. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)
source_refs: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction

options.text: Insert a femoral central line and commence therapeutic anticoagulation for venous obstruction
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is indicated when obstruction is caused by catheter associated thrombosis, which is not the case in a woman with no line and an obvious mediastinal mass. Extrinsic compression by tumour does not respond to anticoagulation. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)
source_refs: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction

options.text: Arrange outpatient respiratory clinic review in two weeks with bronchoscopy at that appointment
options.rationale: Although she is currently stable, obstruction with established collateral circulation and a new mass warrants inpatient workup because deterioration can be rapid and the diagnostic pathway needs to run in days. A two week outpatient wait is too slow for a syndrome with this trajectory. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)
source_refs: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction

options.text: Refer for immediate endovascular stenting of the obstructed vein before establishing the diagnosis
options.rationale: Stenting gives rapid relief and is the right choice for severe or refractory symptoms, particularly airway compromise or cerebral oedema, but it is not required first in a patient who is stable with a normal conscious state. Proceeding to stent before tissue diagnosis also commits her to antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy that can complicate an urgent biopsy. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)
source_refs: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction

options.text: Perform contrast computed tomography of the chest and arrange urgent tissue sampling of the mass
options.rationale: Contrast imaging defines the level and cause of the obstruction, shows the collateral circulation and identifies the safest target for sampling, while histology determines whether the tumour is one that responds rapidly to systemic therapy. Since she is stable with no airway or neurological compromise, there is time to obtain the diagnosis that dictates every subsequent treatment decision. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)
source_refs: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction

explanation.summary: Obstruction of the superior vena cava presents with facial and upper limb swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins and visible chest wall collaterals, characteristically worse on bending forward or lying flat. Malignancy causes the majority of cases, most often lung cancer or lymphoma, although catheter associated thrombosis is an increasingly common benign cause. It is only a true emergency when there is stridor or airway compromise, or cerebral oedema with altered conscious state, and in the stable patient the priority is a contrast computed tomography followed by urgent tissue diagnosis. Treating with radiotherapy before biopsy risks rendering histology uninterpretable and may deny the patient the correct systemic therapy, while endovascular stenting is reserved for severe or refractory symptoms.
key_points: Facial swelling worse on bending, with non-pulsatile distended neck veins and chest wall collaterals
Stridor or altered conscious state converts this into a true emergency needing immediate intervention
Obtain tissue before radiotherapy so that chemosensitive tumours can be identified
Anticoagulation treats catheter associated thrombosis, not extrinsic compression by tumour
explanation.pearls: Stable superior vena cava obstruction buys you the days needed for a diagnosis: get contrast computed tomography and tissue first, because radiotherapy given before biopsy can render the histology uninterpretable and cost the patient the chemotherapy that a lymphoma or small cell carcinoma would have responded to.

sources.label: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction
Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: watery diarrhoea eight weeks into immunotherapy with negative stool studies and rectal bleeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 61-year-old man who has received four cycles of pembrolizumab for metastatic melanoma over eight weeks. He describes nine days of watery diarrhoea, now eight to ten times daily including twice overnight, with cramping and streaks of fresh blood in the stool.

He has lost 4 kg. He has not travelled, has taken no antibiotics and no new medications, and no one else at home is unwell. He has no fever and no vomiting. Stool microscopy and culture, a nucleic acid test for Clostridioides difficile toxin and a stool viral panel are all negative. Computed tomography of the abdomen shows diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and pericolic stranding, with no perforation, no abscess and no obstruction. His melanoma has responded, with reduction in the size of the liver and lung deposits on the same scan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), stool cultures and Clostridioides difficile toxin negative
data_table.Imaging: Diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and pericolic stranding, no perforation or abscess
data_table.Treatment history: Four cycles of pembrolizumab over eight weeks with radiological response of metastatic disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start loperamide with oral rehydration and continue the next cycle of immunotherapy as scheduled
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are appropriate for low grade diarrhoea without alarm features, but with ten stools daily, nocturnal symptoms and blood they risk masking progression toward toxic dilatation and perforation. Continuing the drug during active grade three toxicity compounds the injury. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity

options.text: Withhold the immunotherapy and start high dose intravenous methylprednisolone with early gastroenterology review
options.rationale: Colitis of this severity from checkpoint inhibition is treated as an immune mediated injury with the drug withheld and high dose corticosteroid started without waiting, since delay increases the risk of perforation and of steroid refractory disease. Gastroenterology involvement allows early flexible sigmoidoscopy to confirm the diagnosis and grade the mucosal injury, and identifies those who will need infliximab or vedolizumab if there is no response within three days. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity

options.text: Give empirical oral vancomycin for presumed Clostridioides difficile infection despite the negative test
options.rationale: Repeat or empirical treatment is reasonable when pretest probability is high, such as after recent antibiotics or hospitalisation, and neither applies here with a negative toxin test. Treating an infection he does not have delays the immunosuppression that this colitis requires. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Clostridioides difficile infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Clostridioides difficile infection

options.text: Begin infliximab immediately as first line therapy, bypassing corticosteroids to prevent perforation
options.rationale: Infliximab is the standard second line agent for colitis that does not respond to corticosteroids within about three days, and skipping the steroid trial exposes most patients to a biologic they would not have needed. It is also contraindicated until perforation and infection have been excluded, which requires the assessment described in the correct option. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity

options.text: Cease the immunotherapy permanently and provide supportive care only with no immunosuppression
options.rationale: Stopping the drug is necessary but insufficient, because the inflammatory process continues for weeks after the last dose given the long duration of receptor occupancy. Supportive care alone leaves a patient at real risk of perforation. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity

explanation.summary: Immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis typically appears within the first few months of treatment and is graded by stool frequency above baseline together with features such as nocturnal stools, blood, pain and dehydration. Infection must be excluded, since the treatment is immunosuppression, but once stool studies are negative and imaging shows diffuse colitis the diagnosis is made clinically. Severe disease is managed by withholding the checkpoint inhibitor and starting high dose intravenous corticosteroid immediately, with flexible sigmoidoscopy to confirm and grade the mucosal injury. Failure to improve within about three days defines steroid refractory disease and prompts infliximab, or vedolizumab where a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor is undesirable, and steroids are then tapered slowly over four to six weeks because rapid tapering causes relapse.
key_points: Exclude infection first, then treat severe colitis as an immune mediated injury without further delay
Withhold the checkpoint inhibitor and give high dose intravenous corticosteroid
Lack of response within about three days defines steroid refractory disease and prompts infliximab
Taper corticosteroids over four to six weeks, since rapid reduction causes relapse
explanation.pearls: Nocturnal stools and blood are the features that move checkpoint inhibitor diarrhoea out of the loperamide category: once stool studies are negative, withhold the drug and start high dose intravenous methylprednisolone the same day, and if there is no improvement by day three, escalate to infliximab rather than waiting out the steroid.

sources.label: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Clostridioides difficile infection

subtopic_detail: hot swollen midfoot with intact skin and normal inflammatory markers in long standing neuropathy
stem:
You are the doctor in a diabetes clinic. A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes of 19 years duration reports three weeks of a swollen, red, warm right foot. He has continued walking on it and working as a delivery driver throughout.

He has dense peripheral neuropathy and cannot feel the 10 g monofilament anywhere on either foot. He describes only a dull ache rather than pain. The right midfoot is swollen and about 4 degrees Celsius warmer than the left on infrared measurement, with intact skin, no ulcer, no break in the skin anywhere and no discharge. Foot pulses are easily palpable and his toe pressures are normal. He is systemically well and afebrile. Plain radiographs of the foot are reported as showing no fracture and no bone destruction, and blood tests taken today have returned. The swelling is reduced but not abolished when the foot is elevated for ten minutes.

data_table.Examination: Swollen erythematous right midfoot 4 degrees Celsius warmer than the left, intact skin with no ulcer, palpable pedal pulses, absent monofilament sensation bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), glycated haemoglobin 8.1 per cent
data_table.Imaging: Plain radiographs reported as showing no fracture and no bone destruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for two weeks and review the foot in the clinic afterwards
options.rationale: Cellulitis requires a portal of entry and is usually accompanied by systemic features or raised inflammatory markers, and here the skin is intact with a C-reactive protein of 4 mg/L. Antibiotics would allow continued weight bearing through an unstable foot for another fortnight. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

options.text: Start colchicine and check a serum urate level, treating this as an acute crystal arthropathy
options.rationale: Acute gout is intensely painful even in the presence of neuropathy and characteristically affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint rather than producing diffuse midfoot warmth and swelling over three weeks. The painless, indolent course does not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Gout)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Gout

options.text: Arrange compression stockings and diuretics for presumed dependent oedema of the lower limb
options.rationale: Dependent oedema is bilateral, painless, cool and resolves substantially with elevation, whereas this foot is unilateral, several degrees warmer than the other side and only partly improved by elevation. Compression over an unrecognised unstable foot risks skin breakdown. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

options.text: Refer urgently for vascular assessment and angiography given the unilateral erythema and swelling
options.rationale: Critical limb ischaemia presents with rest pain, pallor on elevation, absent pulses and tissue loss, and his pulses and toe pressures are normal. Pursuing revascularisation would delay the offloading that protects the foot architecture. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

options.text: Immobilise in a total contact cast with no weight bearing and arrange magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: A hot swollen foot in a person with dense neuropathy and intact skin is active Charcot neuroarthropathy until proven otherwise, and plain radiographs are normal in the earliest stage when intervention matters most. Immediate offloading in a total contact cast prevents the collapse that produces a rocker bottom deformity and subsequent ulceration, and magnetic resonance imaging detects the bone marrow oedema that confirms the diagnosis. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

explanation.summary: Active Charcot neuroarthropathy presents as a warm, swollen, erythematous foot in a person with dense peripheral neuropathy and good arterial supply, often with minimal pain and no systemic illness. A temperature difference of more than two degrees Celsius between the feet, in the presence of intact skin and normal inflammatory markers, is the key discriminator from infection. Plain radiographs are normal in the early stage, which is exactly when offloading changes the outcome, so a normal film must never be used to exclude the diagnosis, and magnetic resonance imaging showing bone marrow oedema is the confirmatory test. Treatment is immediate immobilisation in a total contact cast with avoidance of weight bearing, continued for months and guided by resolution of the temperature difference, because continued walking on the affected foot causes midfoot collapse, deformity and eventual ulceration.
key_points: A skin temperature difference above two degrees Celsius with intact skin suggests Charcot rather than infection
Normal radiographs are expected early and do not exclude the diagnosis
Immediate total contact casting and offloading prevents irreversible midfoot collapse
Magnetic resonance imaging showing bone marrow oedema confirms active disease
explanation.pearls: Measure both feet with an infrared thermometer whenever a neuropathic foot is swollen: more than two degrees Celsius of difference with unbroken skin and a normal C-reactive protein means active Charcot neuroarthropathy, and the cast goes on that day rather than after the magnetic resonance scan is reported.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease
Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Gout

subtopic_detail: sudden proximal limb paralysis on waking after a carbohydrate heavy meal with a suppressed thyrotropin
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 28-year-old man is brought in at 6 am unable to stand. He woke unable to lift his legs off the bed and could not get out of bed unaided, having eaten a large rice and noodle meal and played indoor soccer the previous evening.

He is fully alert and oriented, speaks normally, swallows without difficulty and has no diplopia, no ptosis and no facial weakness. Power is 2 out of 5 in both hip flexors and 3 out of 5 in both shoulder abductors, with distal power preserved at 5 out of 5 and reflexes reduced symmetrically. Sensation is entirely normal throughout, with no sensory level. He has lost 5 kg over three months despite a good appetite, and reports palpitations and heat intolerance. He has a fine tremor and a small smooth non-tender goitre. There is no family history of similar episodes, no diarrhoea, no diuretic or corticosteroid use, and no recent vomiting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 142/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 2.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.85 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), phosphate 0.6 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110), thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free thyroxine 38 pmol/L (10-20)
data_table.Examination: Proximal weakness with preserved distal power, reduced reflexes, normal sensation, fine tremor, small smooth goitre
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia with flattened T waves and prominent U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Rapid potassium replacement at 40 mmol per hour until the serum potassium exceeds 4.0 mmol/L
options.rationale: The potassium here has shifted into cells rather than being lost from the body, so aggressive replacement is followed by rebound hyperkalaemia as the shift reverses, which has caused fatal arrhythmias in this syndrome. Replacement is given cautiously in small increments with frequent measurement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin for presumed acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy
options.rationale: Guillain-Barre syndrome produces ascending weakness with areflexia over days, usually with sensory symptoms and often autonomic involvement, and does not cause a potassium of 2.1 mmol/L. The abrupt overnight onset with profound hypokalaemia points elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Neuromuscular disorders)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Neuromuscular disorders

options.text: Urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the spinal cord to exclude an acute compressive lesion
options.rationale: Cord compression produces a sensory level, sphincter disturbance and upper motor neurone signs below the lesion, none of which are present, and it does not explain a symmetrical proximal pattern with normal sensation. Imaging would delay treatment of a rapidly correctable metabolic cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Neuromuscular disorders)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Neuromuscular disorders

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate followed by insulin with dextrose to stabilise the cardiac membrane
options.rationale: This is the treatment for hyperkalaemia, and insulin would drive even more potassium into cells and deepen the paralysis in a man whose potassium is already 2.1 mmol/L. The electrocardiographic changes described are those of hypokalaemia with U waves rather than of hyperkalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis

options.text: Cautious potassium replacement with a non-selective beta blocker and treatment of the thyrotoxicosis
options.rationale: The weakness comes from potassium shifting into muscle cells under the combined drive of thyroid hormone excess, insulin release after a carbohydrate load and exercise, so small cautious potassium doses restore power while avoiding the rebound hyperkalaemia that follows overcorrection. A non-selective beta blocker blocks the beta adrenergic drive of that shift and often reverses the paralysis, and definitive prevention requires rendering him euthyroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis

explanation.summary: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is a shift hypokalaemia in which thyroid hormone excess amplifies sodium potassium pump activity, so that insulin release after a carbohydrate load, rest after exercise, or a high salt meal precipitates sudden proximal weakness. It occurs predominantly in young men, is most common in patients of Asian background, and may be the first manifestation of thyrotoxicosis. Because total body potassium is normal, aggressive replacement leads to rebound hyperkalaemia once the shift reverses, and deaths have resulted, so replacement is given in small cautious doses with frequent monitoring. A non-selective beta blocker such as propranolol counteracts the adrenergic drive and often reverses the attack, while definitive prevention depends on treating the underlying thyrotoxicosis.
key_points: Sudden proximal weakness with normal sensation and profound hypokalaemia suggests a shift rather than a loss
Carbohydrate loads, rest after exercise and high salt meals are typical precipitants
Aggressive potassium replacement causes rebound hyperkalaemia because total body stores are normal
A non-selective beta blocker often aborts the attack, and definitive treatment is of the thyrotoxicosis
explanation.pearls: Check a thyroid stimulating hormone in any young man with sudden painless proximal weakness and a potassium under 2.5 mmol/L: the potassium has shifted rather than been lost, so replace it in small cautious increments alongside propranolol, and expect rebound hyperkalaemia if you infuse it as you would for a diuretic induced deficit.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis
Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Neuromuscular disorders

subtopic_detail: new jaundice with tender hepatomegaly after decades of heavy drinking and a markedly raised discriminant function
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 51-year-old man with three weeks of deepening jaundice, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort. He drinks about 20 standard drinks daily and his last drink was two days ago.

He has no fever, no abdominal pain on movement and no confusion, and he is oriented with no asterixis. The liver edge is smooth and tender 4 cm below the costal margin, there is no ascites clinically and no shifting dullness. Abdominal ultrasound shows a slightly enlarged echogenic liver with patent hepatic and portal veins, no biliary dilatation and no gallstones. Screening for hepatitis A, B and C, autoimmune markers, ferritin studies and caeruloplasmin are all negative or normal. Blood cultures, chest radiograph, urinalysis and an ascitic tap are not indicated or are negative, and he is on no regular medication, including no paracetamol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 290 micromol/L (less than 20), aspartate aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 35), international normalised ratio 2.1 with a control of 1.0, creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)
data_table.Imaging: Enlarged echogenic liver with patent hepatic and portal veins, no biliary dilatation or gallstones
data_table.Screening: Viral hepatitis serology, autoimmune markers, iron studies and caeruloplasmin negative or normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment decision now?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone with screening for infection and a planned response check at day seven
options.rationale: A discriminant function above 32, calculated from the prothrombin time prolongation and the bilirubin, defines severe disease with a high short term mortality, and corticosteroid is the only therapy shown to improve survival in that group. Infection must be excluded or treated first because it is the main contraindication, and the day seven response score determines whether to continue the course or stop it as futile. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Give N-acetylcysteine as an infusion for presumed paracetamol related hepatic injury
options.rationale: Paracetamol toxicity produces transaminases in the thousands with a comparatively low bilirubin early on, and he takes none. N-acetylcysteine has been studied as an adjunct in this condition but is not the primary treatment decision here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology, Paracetamol poisoning)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology, Paracetamol poisoning

options.text: Begin empirical piperacillin with tazobactam and defer specific liver treatment for 48 hours
options.rationale: A raised white cell count is expected in this condition and is not by itself evidence of infection in an afebrile man with a negative screen. Empirical antibiotics without a source delay a time-critical treatment decision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Arrange urgent transjugular liver biopsy before committing him to any specific drug therapy
options.rationale: Biopsy confirms the diagnosis and is used where the history or biochemistry is ambiguous, but here the drinking history, the ratio of aminotransferases and the exclusion of other causes make it unnecessary. Waiting for a procedure would delay treatment in a condition with high short term mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Provide thiamine, nutrition and withdrawal management alone, with review in the liver clinic
options.rationale: Abstinence, thiamine, withdrawal management and aggressive nutritional support are essential in every case and improve outcomes, but on their own they do not address the mortality risk that defines severe disease. They accompany corticosteroid rather than replacing it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease

explanation.summary: Alcohol related hepatitis presents with rapid onset jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and a neutrophil leucocytosis on a background of sustained heavy drinking, with aspartate aminotransferase characteristically higher than alanine aminotransferase and rarely exceeding about 300 U/L. Severity is quantified by the discriminant function derived from the prothrombin time and bilirubin, with a value above 32 marking severe disease and high short term mortality. Corticosteroid therapy improves short term survival in that group, provided active infection, gastrointestinal bleeding and significant renal failure have been addressed, and response is reassessed at day seven using a composite score so that non-responders are not continued on futile immunosuppression. Abstinence, thiamine, withdrawal management and nutritional support are given to every patient regardless of severity and are the interventions that determine long term outcome.
key_points: Aspartate aminotransferase exceeds alanine aminotransferase and is rarely above 300 U/L
A discriminant function above 32 defines severe disease with high short term mortality
Exclude and treat infection before starting corticosteroid, since it is the main contraindication
Reassess response at day seven and stop steroid in non-responders
explanation.pearls: Calculate the discriminant function before deciding anything in alcohol related hepatitis: a value above 32 identifies the patients for whom corticosteroid improves short term survival, and the same calculation tells you to reassess at day seven and stop rather than continue immunosuppressing a non-responder.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease
Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology, Paracetamol poisoning

subtopic_detail: quotidian fevers with an evanescent salmon rash and sore throat in a young adult with extreme hyperferritinaemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar with a 27-year-old woman admitted for the second time in six weeks with fever. Her temperature spikes to 39.5 degrees Celsius once each evening and returns to normal by morning without antipyretics.

During the spikes a salmon coloured rash appears over her trunk and thighs and fades within hours, so it has been absent at each previous review. She has a persistent sore throat with a normal looking pharynx, aching in both wrists and knees, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Two sets of blood cultures on each admission have been negative and she has had no response to a week of intravenous ceftriaxone. Transthoracic echocardiography shows no vegetation, computed tomography of the chest abdomen and pelvis shows only mild splenomegaly and small reactive nodes, antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor are negative, and a viral panel including Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus and human immunodeficiency virus is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.5 degrees Celsius during a spike
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with 88 per cent neutrophils, C-reactive protein 190 mg/L (less than 5), ferritin 9800 micrograms/L (30-300), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 35)
data_table.Serology: Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor negative, blood cultures negative on four sets, viral panel negative
data_table.Imaging: Echocardiogram without vegetation, computed tomography showing mild splenomegaly and small reactive nodes

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Culture negative infective endocarditis requiring extended incubation and serological testing
options.rationale: Endocarditis would be supported by a new murmur, embolic phenomena or vegetations, and the echocardiogram is clear after two admissions and a week of ceftriaxone without response. It also does not produce a rash that appears only with the fever spike. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease

options.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with fever, arthralgia and a photosensitive eruption
options.rationale: Lupus is effectively excluded by a negative antinuclear antibody, and it characteristically causes leucopenia rather than a neutrophil count of 21.6 x10^9/L. Its rash is fixed and photosensitive rather than evanescent with fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Systemic lupus erythematosus)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Systemic lupus erythematosus

options.text: Lymphoma with B symptoms, which would account for fevers, splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy
options.rationale: Lymphoma remains an important consideration in prolonged fever with splenomegaly and is the reason tissue sampling is often pursued, but the once daily fever pattern with a fever linked evanescent rash and a ferritin near 10000 micrograms/L is not its usual behaviour. Nodes here are small and reactive rather than bulky. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease

options.text: Acute rheumatic fever following an untreated group A streptococcal pharyngeal infection
options.rationale: Acute rheumatic fever requires evidence of preceding streptococcal infection and produces a migratory large joint arthritis with carditis, chorea or erythema marginatum, which is a ring shaped rather than salmon coloured eruption. Neither the serology nor the echocardiogram supports it. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for acute rheumatic fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for acute rheumatic fever

options.text: Adult onset Still disease, a systemic autoinflammatory disorder diagnosed after exclusion
options.rationale: The combination of once daily fever spikes, an evanescent salmon rash appearing only with the fever, arthralgia, sore throat with a normal pharynx, neutrophil leucocytosis, transaminitis and a ferritin in the thousands is the recognised pattern of this disorder. Negative cultures, serology and imaging complete the diagnosis, which is made by exclusion and is treated with corticosteroids and then interleukin 1 or interleukin 6 directed therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease

explanation.summary: Adult onset Still disease is a systemic autoinflammatory disorder whose defining pattern is a daily fever spike returning to baseline, a salmon coloured rash that appears with the fever and fades as it settles, arthralgia or arthritis, and sore throat with an unremarkable pharynx. Laboratory findings include a neutrophil predominant leucocytosis, high inflammatory markers, transaminitis and a strikingly elevated ferritin, often more than five times the upper limit, with a low glycosylated fraction. Because it has no confirmatory test, the diagnosis requires exclusion of infection, malignancy and other connective tissue disease, which is why repeated cultures, echocardiography, cross sectional imaging and autoantibodies all feature in the workup. The major complication to watch for is macrophage activation syndrome, signalled by falling cell counts, falling fibrinogen, rising triglycerides and a further ferritin rise, and treatment begins with corticosteroids before moving to interleukin 1 or interleukin 6 blockade.
key_points: The rash appears only with the fever spike, so it is missed on routine daytime ward rounds
Ferritin is typically in the thousands with a neutrophil predominant leucocytosis
Negative antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor support rather than refute the diagnosis
Watch for macrophage activation syndrome with falling counts and fibrinogen and rising triglycerides
explanation.pearls: Ask nursing staff to look at the skin at the moment of the temperature spike rather than on the morning round: the salmon rash of adult onset Still disease is present only during the fever, and pairing that with a ferritin in the thousands and a neutrophil leucocytosis is what turns a prolonged fever workup into a diagnosis.

subtopic_detail: sensory ataxia with brisk knee reflexes and absent ankle jerks in a young adult using recreational gas canisters
stem:
You are the neurology registrar. A 22-year-old man reports six weeks of numbness and tingling in his feet that has climbed to mid calf, with unsteadiness that is much worse in the dark and in the shower with his eyes closed.

He uses whipped cream chargers recreationally, inhaling up to 50 canisters on a weekend night for the past eight months. He does not drink alcohol, uses no other substances, eats a mixed diet including meat, and takes no medication. On examination vibration and joint position sense are markedly reduced to the knees, pinprick is reduced in a stocking distribution, knee reflexes are brisk with an extensor plantar response on the right, and ankle jerks are absent. Romberg test is positive. Power is 4 plus out of 5 in ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally, and there are no cranial nerve signs, no bladder symptoms and no cognitive change.

data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration and proprioception to the knees, brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle jerks, right extensor plantar, positive Romberg test
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 104 fL (80-100), serum vitamin B12 210 pmol/L (150-700), homocysteine 42 micromol/L (less than 15), methylmalonic acid elevated
data_table.Substance use: Up to 50 nitrous oxide canisters per weekend night for eight months, no alcohol or other substances

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral thiamine and refer to a drug and alcohol service for assessment of alcohol use
options.rationale: Thiamine deficiency causes a painful predominantly sensory neuropathy or Wernicke encephalopathy, and he does not drink alcohol or have ocular or cognitive signs. It also would not explain the dorsal column and corticospinal involvement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before treatment to characterise the neuropathy fully
options.rationale: Electrophysiology will describe the axonal and demyelinating components but changes nothing about the immediate treatment, and the combination of upper and lower motor neurone signs already localises the lesion to cord and nerve. Delaying replacement risks irreversible cord damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy

options.text: Prescribe pregabalin for neuropathic symptoms and review him in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Symptomatic neuropathic agents may help the paraesthesiae but do nothing about the ongoing functional deficiency that is damaging the cord. Six weeks of continued exposure without replacement risks permanent disability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy

options.text: Give intravenous methylprednisolone for a presumed first demyelinating event of the spinal cord
options.rationale: A demyelinating event would produce a sensory level and would not be accompanied by macrocytosis with a raised homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. Corticosteroids would leave the metabolic cause untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Multiple sclerosis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Multiple sclerosis

options.text: Cease the inhalant use and start parenteral hydroxocobalamin with neurology follow up
options.rationale: Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt core of cobalamin, so the vitamin is present in serum but functionally inactive, which is why the level looks near normal while homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are elevated. Treatment is to stop the exposure and give parenteral replacement promptly, since the combined degeneration of dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts becomes irreversible if it persists. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy

explanation.summary: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin by oxidising its cobalt centre, producing a functional deficiency that damages the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts as well as peripheral nerves. The characteristic examination finding is a mixture of upper and lower motor neurone signs, with brisk knee reflexes and extensor plantars alongside absent ankle jerks, together with sensory ataxia that worsens without visual input. Serum vitamin B12 is often normal or borderline because the molecule is present but non-functional, so elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are the tests that reveal the deficiency, and macrocytosis may or may not be present. Management is immediate cessation of exposure with parenteral hydroxocobalamin, since recovery depends heavily on how long the deficiency has persisted, and a magnetic resonance scan of the cord may show the inverted V sign of dorsal column signal change.
key_points: Brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle jerks signals combined cord and peripheral nerve involvement
Serum vitamin B12 may be normal because the molecule is inactivated rather than depleted
Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are the tests that establish functional deficiency
Cessation plus prompt parenteral replacement determines whether the deficits reverse
explanation.pearls: A normal serum vitamin B12 does not exclude functional deficiency in nitrous oxide users: send homocysteine and methylmalonic acid, and start parenteral hydroxocobalamin the same day, because dorsal column and corticospinal damage becomes permanent the longer the exposure continues.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Multiple sclerosis

subtopic_detail: unilateral neck pain with a small pupil and droopy lid days before focal weakness in a young adult
stem:
You are the stroke registrar. A 38-year-old woman presents with 40 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech that has now almost resolved, leaving only mild clumsiness of the right hand.

Five days ago she developed left sided neck pain and a headache behind the left eye after a heavy session at the gym doing overhead lifts, and her partner noticed that her left eyelid looked lower. On examination there is mild left ptosis with a small left pupil that reacts to light, and no anhidrosis of the face. Power in the right arm is 5 minus out of 5 with a mild pronator drift and there is no facial droop now. Computed tomography of the brain is normal with no haemorrhage. Her blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, she has no history of hypertension or diabetes, is a non-smoker, and an electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with no atrial fibrillation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild left ptosis with a reactive small left pupil, no facial anhidrosis, right pronator drift with power 5 minus out of 5, speech now normal
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast computed tomography of the brain normal with no haemorrhage
data_table.History: Left neck and periorbital pain for five days following overhead weight lifting, no vascular risk factors

lead_in: Which investigation should you request now?

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography with a bubble study looking for a patent foramen ovale
options.rationale: Paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale is a genuine consideration in young stroke and echocardiography belongs in the workup, but it does not explain unilateral neck pain with an ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome. It would also not change acute management today. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage given the headache
options.rationale: Xanthochromia testing follows a suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with sudden maximal headache and a normal early scan, whereas her headache has been present for five days alongside focal deficit and a Horner syndrome. The pattern points to a vessel wall problem rather than to blood in the subarachnoid space. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Computed tomography angiography of the neck and intracranial vessels performed immediately
options.rationale: Neck pain with an ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome and subsequent cerebral ischaemia in a young person without vascular risk factors is arterial dissection, where a torn intimal layer produces a mural haematoma that stretches the sympathetic fibres running along the vessel and generates embolus. Angiography of the neck vessels is the test that demonstrates it and determines whether antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is chosen. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Temporal artery ultrasound and an urgent erythrocyte sedimentation rate for suspected arteritis
options.rationale: Giant cell arteritis causes headache with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual loss, and it occurs in people over 50 rather than in a 38-year-old. It does not produce a Horner syndrome or follow a mechanical precipitant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Giant cell arteritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Giant cell arteritis

options.text: Prolonged ambulatory cardiac monitoring for 14 days to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
options.rationale: Extended rhythm monitoring is standard for cryptogenic stroke once structural and arterial causes have been excluded, and it is appropriate later in this workup. Starting with it would miss an arterial lesion that is actively embolising and needs a treatment decision today. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

explanation.summary: Cervical artery dissection is a leading cause of stroke in adults under 50 and characteristically produces local pain days before the ischaemic event, giving a window in which the diagnosis can be made. In internal carotid dissection the mural haematoma compresses the sympathetic fibres travelling on the vessel wall, producing a partial Horner syndrome with ptosis and miosis but preserved facial sweating, because the sudomotor fibres travel with the external carotid. Trivial mechanical precipitants such as heavy lifting, sporting neck movement or coughing are common, and there is often no conventional vascular risk factor. Diagnosis rests on computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography of the neck vessels, and antithrombotic treatment with either an antiplatelet agent or anticoagulation is given for three to six months with repeat imaging.
key_points: Pain typically precedes the ischaemic event by days, which is the window for diagnosis
Ptosis and miosis with preserved facial sweating localises the lesion to the internal carotid wall
Minor mechanical precipitants are common and conventional vascular risk factors are often absent
Vessel imaging of the neck rather than cardiac workup is the immediate priority
explanation.pearls: In any stroke or transient ischaemic attack under 50, ask about neck or facial pain in the preceding fortnight and look specifically for a small pupil with a droopy lid on the painful side. Ptosis and miosis with normal facial sweating means carotid dissection, and the next test is angiography of the neck vessels rather than an echocardiogram.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

subtopic_detail: prolonged fever with hepatitis in an abattoir worker after calving season with negative routine cultures
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 44-year-old man with three weeks of daily fevers, drenching sweats, severe headache and profound fatigue. He has lost 6 kg and describes muscle aches across his shoulders and thighs.

He works at an abattoir in regional Queensland and also helps at a neighbouring property, where he assisted with several calvings six weeks ago and disposed of placental material. He has not travelled overseas, has no sick contacts, and has not been bitten by a tick or mosquito that he noticed. Examination shows a temperature of 38.9 degrees Celsius with a soft non-tender abdomen, no rash, no lymphadenopathy and no murmur. Two sets of blood cultures taken a week apart are negative. Chest radiograph is clear, and abdominal ultrasound shows a normal liver and spleen with no focal lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 132 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 35), alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L (30-110), C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Microbiology: Two sets of blood cultures a week apart negative, chest radiograph clear
data_table.Exposure history: Abattoir work in regional Queensland, assisted with calvings and disposed of placental material six weeks ago

lead_in: Which test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Thick and thin blood films examined for malarial parasites on three separate occasions
options.rationale: Malaria requires travel to an endemic area, and Australia has been free of local transmission for decades, so films would be negative in a man who has not left the country. Fever with sweats alone is not enough to justify this pathway without exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to investigate a possible haematological malignancy
options.rationale: Marrow examination is a reasonable late step in prolonged fever of unknown origin, particularly with cytopenias, but it is invasive and the exposure history here points to a specific treatable infection with a simple serological test. The mild thrombocytopenia and transaminitis fit that infection well. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever

options.text: Positron emission tomography to localise a focus of occult infection or inflammation
options.rationale: Functional imaging has a role in prolonged fever after first line investigations have failed, and it may identify vascular or bone infection. Using it before serology for an occupationally acquired pathogen that is easy to diagnose and treat inverts the order of investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever

options.text: Transoesophageal echocardiography to exclude culture negative infective endocarditis
options.rationale: Endocarditis would be suggested by a murmur, embolic phenomena or a predisposing valve lesion, none of which are present in this man. It is worth revisiting if the illness becomes chronic, since the pathogen suggested by his exposure can itself cause endocarditis months later. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever

options.text: Paired serology for Coxiella burnetii taken now and repeated two to three weeks later
options.rationale: Abattoir work and assisting with calving are the classic Australian exposures for Q fever, whose organism is shed in enormous numbers in birth products and inhaled as an aerosol, and which does not grow in routine blood culture bottles. A fourfold rise between paired samples confirms acute infection, and doxycycline is started on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for the second sample. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever

explanation.summary: Q fever is an occupational infection of abattoir workers, farmers, shearers and veterinarians, acquired by inhaling aerosols from birth products, particularly placental material, where the organism is shed in vast quantities. The acute illness is a prolonged febrile syndrome with severe headache, sweats and myalgia, frequently accompanied by a hepatitis and mild thrombocytopenia, and routine blood cultures are always negative because the organism does not grow in standard media. Diagnosis is serological, with paired samples two to three weeks apart demonstrating a fourfold rise, and treatment is doxycycline for two weeks started on clinical suspicion. Australia has a licensed vaccine that requires pre-vaccination skin testing and serology to exclude prior exposure, and it is recommended for at risk occupational groups, while a small proportion of untreated patients develop chronic infection presenting as endocarditis or vascular infection months to years later.
key_points: Exposure to birth products from livestock is the classic route, not necessarily contact with sick animals
Routine blood cultures are negative because the organism does not grow in standard media
Paired serology two to three weeks apart is the diagnostic test, with doxycycline started on suspicion
Vaccination requires prior skin testing and serology, and is recommended for at risk occupations
explanation.pearls: Ask a febrile abattoir or farm worker whether they were present at any births or handled placental material: Q fever is acquired from birth product aerosols, cannot be cultured from blood, and needs paired serology plus doxycycline started on suspicion rather than another set of blood cultures.
